## One architectural correction I would make now

I would **not** call the pure machine “mathematically locked” after differential testing alone.

The stronger and more defensible claim is:

> **The implementation is observationally equivalent to the independently implemented executable reference model over the tested generated state space, subject to the generator's coverage and the reference model's correctness.**

Then, where feasible, we add algebraic properties and the substitution evaluator as a second independent semantic oracle.

That distinction matters for a high-assurance system: **differential testing is powerful evidence, but it is not a formal proof of the implementation.**

With Phase 10 frozen this way, the next boundary is clean:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Pure CEK}
\rightarrow
\text{Capability Semantics}
}
\]

and **`Attenuate` should be Phase 11, before `Request`**. At that point the evaluator does not yet touch the host or consume external-effect budgets; it only asks the capability kernel to derive a strictly weaker opaque `CapRef`. That makes `Attenuate` the ideal first test of the evaluator/kernel boundary.

---

## [26] USER

This is the exact level of rigor required. Your correction regarding `Expr::Value` is fundamental: in a true CEK machine, a value is only terminal if the continuation is empty. Routing *all* values through `continue_with_value` is the single most important invariant for ensuring continuation preservation and deterministic resumption.

Furthermore, your philosophical correction is spot-on: we are establishing **observational equivalence to an independently implemented executable reference model**, which is powerful, empirically verifiable evidence, not a substitute for a formal mathematical proof. We will state it exactly that way.

Below is the **Phase 10 Frozen Implementation (Lambda / Call)**, incorporating the strict left-to-right evaluation, lexical capture, pre-argument arity checking, and the independent reference model.

---

### 1. Updated Instrumentation Events

We expand `MachineEvent` to capture the granular steps of function application for trace equivalence testing.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 28 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MachineEvent {
    EnterLet(Symbol),
    EnterSeq,
    EnterIf,
    EnterCall,
    EnterLambda,
    
    BeginArgument(usize), // Index of argument being evaluated
    EndArgument(usize),
    ApplyFunction,
    
    EvaluateValue(Value),
    Lookup(Symbol),
    PushFrame,
    PopFrame,
    Halt(Value),
    Fault(Fault),
    Block,
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Fault {
    UnboundVariable(Symbol),
    TypeError { expected: &'static str, actual: &'static str },
    ArityMismatch { expected: usize, actual: usize },
    NotImplemented,
}
```

</details>

### 2. The Production Evaluator (Phases 4–10)

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 175 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub fn step_eval(actor: &mut ActorState) -> MachineEvent {
    let expr = std::mem::replace(&mut actor.eval.expr, Expr::Value(Value::Unit));

    match expr {
        Expr::Value(value) => continue_with_value(actor, value),
        
        Expr::Var(symbol) => {
            match actor.eval.env.lookup(symbol) {
                Some(v) => {
                    actor.eval.expr = Expr::Value(v.clone());
                    MachineEvent::Lookup(symbol)
                }
                None => {
                    actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::UnboundVariable(symbol));
                    MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::UnboundVariable(symbol))
                }
            }
        }

        Expr::Let { name, value, body } => {
            let env = actor.eval.env.clone();
            actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::LetValue { name, body: *body, env });
            actor.eval.expr = *value;
            MachineEvent::EnterLet(name)
        }

        Expr::Seq { first, second } => {
            let env = actor.eval.env.clone();
            actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::Seq { second: *second, env });
            actor.eval.expr = *first;
            MachineEvent::EnterSeq
        }

        Expr::If { condition, then_branch, else_branch } => {
            let env = actor.eval.env.clone();
            actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::If { then_branch: *then_branch, else_branch: *else_branch, env });
            actor.eval.expr = *condition;
            MachineEvent::EnterIf
        }

        Expr::Lambda { params, body } => {
            let closure = Value::Function(FunctionValue {
                params,
                body: Box::new(*body),
                env: actor.eval.env.clone(), // LEXICAL CAPTURE
            });
            actor.eval.expr = Expr::Value(closure);
            MachineEvent::EnterLambda
        }

        Expr::Call { function, args } => {
            let caller_env = actor.eval.env.clone();
            actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::CallFunction { args, env: caller_env });
            actor.eval.expr = *function; // Evaluate function first
            MachineEvent::EnterCall
        }

        _ => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::NotImplemented);
            MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::NotImplemented)
        }
    }
}

// THE SINGLE VALUE-RETURN PATH
fn continue_with_value(actor: &mut ActorState, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    match actor.eval.continuation.pop() {
        None => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Halted(value.clone());
            MachineEvent::Halt(value)
        }
        Some(frame) => resume_frame(actor, frame, value),
    }
}

fn resume_frame(actor: &mut ActorState, frame: Frame, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    match frame {
        Frame::LetValue { name, body, env } => {
            actor.eval.env = env.extend(name, value);
            actor.eval.expr = body;
            MachineEvent::PopFrame
        }
        Frame::Seq { second, env } => {
            actor.eval.env = env;
            actor.eval.expr = second;
            MachineEvent::PopFrame
        }
        Frame::If { then_branch, else_branch, env } => {
            actor.eval.env = env;
            match value {
                Value::Bool(true) => actor.eval.expr = then_branch,
                Value::Bool(false) => actor.eval.expr = else_branch,
                _ => {
                    let fault = Fault::TypeError { expected: "Bool", actual: "non-bool" };
                    actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
                    return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
                }
            }
            MachineEvent::PopFrame
        }
        Frame::CallFunction { args, env: caller_env } => {
            let function = match value {
                Value::Function(f) => f,
                _ => {
                    let fault = Fault::TypeError { expected: "Function", actual: "non-function" };
                    actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
                    return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
                }
            };

            // ARITY CHECK BEFORE ANY ARGUMENT EVALUATION
            if function.params.len() != args.len() {
                let fault = Fault::ArityMismatch {
                    expected: function.params.len(),
                    actual: args.len(),
                };
                actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
                return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
            }

            if args.is_empty() {
                return apply_function(actor, function, Vec::new());
            }

            let mut remaining = args;
            let first = remaining.remove(0);
            
            actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::CallArgument {
                function,
                evaluated: Vec::new(),
                remaining,
                caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
            });
            actor.eval.env = caller_env;
            actor.eval.expr = first;
            
            MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)
        }
        Frame::CallArgument { function, mut evaluated, mut remaining, caller_env } => {
            let arg_idx = evaluated.len();
            evaluated.push(value);
            
            if remaining.is_empty() {
                MachineEvent::EndArgument(arg_idx);
                apply_function(actor, function, evaluated)
            } else {
                let next = remaining.remove(0);
                actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::CallArgument {
                    function,
                    evaluated,
                    remaining,
                    caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
                });
                actor.eval.env = caller_env;
                actor.eval.expr = next;
                
                MachineEvent::EndArgument(arg_idx) // Previous arg ended
                // Note: The next step_eval will emit BeginArgument for the new arg
            }
        }
    }
}

fn apply_function(actor: &mut ActorState, function: FunctionValue, arguments: Vec<Value>) -> MachineEvent {
    // LEXICAL SCOPING: Extend the closure's captured environment, NOT the caller's
    let mut env = function.env.clone();
    for (param, argument) in function.params.into_iter().zip(arguments.into_iter()) {
        env = env.extend(param, argument);
    }
    
    actor.eval.env = env;
    actor.eval.expr = *function.body;
    
    MachineEvent::ApplyFunction
}
```

</details>

### 3. The Independent Reference Model

This model duplicates the logic. It **does not call** `continue_with_value`, `resume_frame`, or `apply_function` from the production code.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 120 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub fn reference_step(state: &mut RefState) -> MachineEvent {
    if state.outcome != RefOutcome::Running {
        return MachineEvent::Halt(Value::Unit);
    }

    match state.expr.clone() {
        Expr::Value(value) => {
            if state.kont.is_empty() {
                state.outcome = RefOutcome::Halted(value.clone());
                MachineEvent::Halt(value)
            } else {
                reference_continue_with_value(state, value)
            }
        }
        // ... (Let, Seq, If, Var identical to previous reference model) ...
        
        Expr::Lambda { params, body } => {
            let closure = Value::Function(FunctionValue {
                params,
                body: Box::new(*body),
                env: state.env.clone(),
            });
            state.expr = Expr::Value(closure);
            MachineEvent::EnterLambda
        }
        
        Expr::Call { function, args } => {
            let caller_env = state.env.clone();
            state.kont.push(Frame::CallFunction { args, env: caller_env });
            state.expr = *function;
            MachineEvent::EnterCall
        }
        _ => {
            state.outcome = RefOutcome::Fault(Fault::NotImplemented);
            MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::NotImplemented)
        }
    }
}

fn reference_continue_with_value(state: &mut RefState, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    match state.kont.pop() {
        None => {
            state.outcome = RefOutcome::Halted(value.clone());
            MachineEvent::Halt(value)
        }
        Some(frame) => reference_resume_frame(state, frame, value),
    }
}

fn reference_resume_frame(state: &mut RefState, frame: Frame, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    match frame {
        Frame::CallFunction { args, env: caller_env } => {
            let function = match value {
                Value::Function(f) => f,
                _ => {
                    state.outcome = RefOutcome::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Function", actual: "non-function" });
                    return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Function", actual: "non-function" });
                }
            };

            if function.params.len() != args.len() {
                let fault = Fault::ArityMismatch { expected: function.params.len(), actual: args.len() };
                state.outcome = RefOutcome::Fault(fault.clone());
                return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
            }

            if args.is_empty() {
                return reference_apply(state, function, Vec::new());
            }

            let mut remaining = args;
            let first = remaining.remove(0);
            
            state.kont.push(Frame::CallArgument {
                function,
                evaluated: Vec::new(),
                remaining,
                caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
            });
            state.env = caller_env;
            state.expr = first;
            
            MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)
        }
        Frame::CallArgument { function, mut evaluated, mut remaining, caller_env } => {
            let arg_idx = evaluated.len();
            evaluated.push(value);
            
            if remaining.is_empty() {
                MachineEvent::EndArgument(arg_idx);
                reference_apply(state, function, evaluated)
            } else {
                let next = remaining.remove(0);
                state.kont.push(Frame::CallArgument {
                    function,
                    evaluated,
                    remaining,
                    caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
                });
                state.env = caller_env;
                state.expr = next;
                MachineEvent::EndArgument(arg_idx)
            }
        }
        // ... (Let, Seq, If handled similarly) ...
        _ => MachineEvent::PopFrame,
    }
}

fn reference_apply(state: &mut RefState, function: FunctionValue, arguments: Vec<Value>) -> MachineEvent {
    let mut env = function.env.clone(); // LEXICAL SCOPING
    for (param, argument) in function.params.into_iter().zip(arguments.into_iter()) {
        env = env.extend(param, argument);
    }
    
    state.env = env;
    state.expr = *function.body;
    
    MachineEvent::ApplyFunction
}
```

</details>

### 4. Phase 10 Property Test Suite

These tests enforce the specific semantic invariants you outlined.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 124 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
proptest! {
    // 1. Lexical Capture Invariant
    #[test]
    fn closures_capture_lexical_environment(
        captured in arb_value(),
        shadowed in arb_value(),
    ) {
        let x = Symbol(1);
        let f = Symbol(2);
        
        // let x = captured in
        //   let f = lambda() x in
        //     let x = shadowed in
        //       f()
        let expr = Expr::Let {
            name: x,
            value: Box::new(Expr::Value(captured.clone())),
            body: Box::new(Expr::Let {
                name: f,
                value: Box::new(Expr::Lambda {
                    params: vec![],
                    body: Box::new(Expr::Var(x)),
                }),
                body: Box::new(Expr::Let {
                    name: x,
                    value: Box::new(Expr::Value(shadowed)),
                    body: Box::new(Expr::Call {
                        function: Box::new(Expr::Var(f)),
                        args: vec![],
                    }),
                }),
            }),
        };

        let (ref_final, _) = run_reference(RefState::new(expr, Environment::empty()), 10_000);
        
        prop_assert_eq!(ref_final.outcome, RefOutcome::Halted(captured));
    }

    // 2. Left-to-Right Argument Evaluation
    #[test]
    fn arguments_evaluate_strictly_left_to_right(
        arg1 in arb_observable_expr(1), // Emits specific trace marker
        arg2 in arb_observable_expr(2),
        arg3 in arb_observable_expr(3),
    ) {
        let expr = Expr::Call {
            function: Box::new(Expr::Lambda {
                params: vec![Symbol(1), Symbol(2), Symbol(3)],
                body: Box::new(Expr::Value(Value::Unit)),
            }),
            args: vec![arg1, arg2, arg3],
        };

        let (_, trace) = run_reference(RefState::new(expr, Environment::empty()), 10_000);
        
        let pos1 = trace.iter().position(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)));
        let pos2 = trace.iter().position(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::BeginArgument(1)));
        let pos3 = trace.iter().position(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::BeginArgument(2)));
        
        prop_assert!(pos1 < pos2 && pos2 < pos3, "Arguments must evaluate strictly left-to-right");
    }

    // 3. Arity Mismatch Prevents Argument Evaluation
    #[test]
    fn arity_mismatch_faults_before_argument_evaluation(
        bad_arg in arb_observable_expr(99), // Would emit marker 99 if evaluated
    ) {
        let expr = Expr::Call {
            function: Box::new(Expr::Lambda {
                params: vec![], // Expects 0 args
                body: Box::new(Expr::Value(Value::Unit)),
            }),
            args: vec![bad_arg], // Providing 1 arg
        };

        let (_, trace) = run_reference(RefState::new(expr, Environment::empty()), 10_000);
        
        let arg_evaluated = trace.iter().any(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)));
        let faulted = trace.iter().any(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::ArityMismatch { .. })));
        
        prop_assert!(!arg_evaluated, "Argument must not be evaluated on arity mismatch");
        prop_assert!(faulted, "Must fault with ArityMismatch");
    }

    // 4. Deep Call Stack Independence
    #[test]
    fn deep_call_machine_avoids_host_recursion() {
        // Construct: f(f(f(...(unit)...))) where f = lambda(x) x
        let depth = 50_000;
        let mut expr = Expr::Value(Value::Unit);
        let f_sym = Symbol(0);
        
        for _ in 0..depth {
            expr = Expr::Call {
                function: Box::new(Expr::Var(f_sym)),
                args: vec![expr],
            };
        }
        
        // Wrap in let f = lambda(x) x in ...
        expr = Expr::Let {
            name: f_sym,
            value: Box::new(Expr::Lambda {
                params: vec![Symbol(1)],
                body: Box::new(Expr::Var(Symbol(1))),
            }),
            body: Box::new(expr),
        };

        let mut actor = test_actor_with_expr(expr);
        let mut steps = 0;
        let max_steps = depth * 10;
        
        while steps < max_steps {
            match step_eval(&mut actor) {
                MachineEvent::Halt(_) => return, // Success
                MachineEvent::Fault(f) => panic!("Unexpected fault: {:?}", f),
                _ => { steps += 1; }
            }
        }
        panic!("Deep call evaluation did not terminate within expected steps");
    }
}
```

### 5. Phase 10 Acceptance Gate Achieved

With this implementation, we have established:
1. **Observational Equivalence**: The production CEK machine and the independent reference model produce identical `MachineEvent` traces and final states across the generated state space.
2. **Lexical Scoping**: Closures strictly capture and use their creation environment.
3. **Deterministic Order**: Arguments evaluate strictly left-to-right, and arity faults abort evaluation *before* any argument is touched.
4. **Stack Independence**: The iterative `step_eval` + `Continuation` vector handles deep nesting without host-language recursion.

### The Path to Phase 11: Attenuate

You are absolutely correct that `Attenuate` must precede `Request`. `Attenuate` is the perfect bridge: it introduces the `CapabilityKernel` boundary, but it is a **pure, internal transition**. It does not consume external-effect budgets, it does not yield to the host, and it does not introduce nondeterminism. 

In Phase 11, we will implement `Expr::Attenuate` such that:
1. It evaluates the `capability` expression to a `Value::Capability(cap_ref)`.
2. It calls `kernel.derive(cap_ref, constraint)`.
3. It pushes a frame to evaluate the `body` in an environment where the new `cap_ref` is bound (or passed directly).
4. It emits no `EffectRequest` and consumes only standard computational fuel.

Shall we draft the Phase 11 `Attenuate` semantics and its specific property tests, establishing the first verified handoff to the Capability Kernel?

# Phase 10: Lambda / Call (Frozen Pure CEK Machine)

## 1. Instrumentation and Frames

We introduce explicit semantic events for the reference oracle to track evaluation order and application boundaries.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 32 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MachineEvent {
    EnterLet(Symbol),
    EnterSeq,
    EnterIf,
    EnterCall,
    EnterLambda,
    BeginArgument(usize), // Index of argument being evaluated
    EndArgument(usize),
    ApplyFunction,
    EvaluateValue(Value),
    Lookup(Symbol),
    PushFrame,
    PopFrame,
    Halt(Value),
    Fault(Fault),
    Block,
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Frame {
    LetValue { name: Symbol, body: Expr, env: Environment },
    Seq { second: Expr, env: Environment },
    If { then_branch: Expr, else_branch: Expr, env: Environment },
    CallFunction { args: Vec<Expr>, env: Environment },
    CallArgument { 
        function: FunctionValue, 
        evaluated: Vec<Value>, 
        remaining: Vec<Expr>, 
        caller_env: Environment, // Crucial: preserved to restore caller state
    },
}
```

</details>

## 2. The Core Value-Return Invariant

This is the mechanical heart of the CEK machine. A value is only terminal if the continuation is empty.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 11 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn continue_with_value(actor: &mut ActorState, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    match actor.eval.continuation.pop() {
        None => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Halted(value.clone());
            MachineEvent::Halt(value)
        }
        Some(frame) => {
            resume_frame(actor, frame, value)
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

## 3. Lambda and Call Transitions

Lambda creation is pure and deterministic. It produces a value that immediately flows through `continue_with_value`.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 22 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn enter_lambda(actor: &mut ActorState, params: Vec<Symbol>, body: Expr) -> MachineEvent {
    let closure = Value::Function(FunctionValue {
        params,
        body: Box::new(body),
        env: actor.eval.env.clone(), // LEXICAL CAPTURE
    });
    
    actor.eval.expr = Expr::Value(closure);
    MachineEvent::EnterLambda
}

fn enter_call(actor: &mut ActorState, function: Expr, args: Vec<Expr>) -> MachineEvent {
    let caller_env = actor.eval.env.clone();
    
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::CallFunction {
        args,
        env: caller_env.clone(),
    });
    
    actor.eval.expr = function; // Evaluate function first
    MachineEvent::EnterCall
}
```

</details>

## 4. Function Return and Arity Check

When the function expression resolves to a value, we check arity *before* evaluating any arguments. This prevents observable side effects in invalid calls.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 44 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn resume_call_function(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    args: Vec<Expr>,
    caller_env: Environment,
    value: Value,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let function = match value {
        Value::Function(f) => f,
        _ => {
            let fault = Fault::TypeError { expected: "Function", actual: "non-function" };
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
        }
    };

    // ARITY CHECK BEFORE ARGUMENT EVALUATION
    if function.params.len() != args.len() {
        let fault = Fault::ArityMismatch {
            expected: function.params.len(),
            actual: args.len(),
        };
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
        return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
    }

    let mut remaining = args;
    if remaining.is_empty() {
        return apply_function(actor, function, Vec::new());
    }

    let first = remaining.remove(0);
    
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::CallArgument {
        function,
        evaluated: Vec::new(),
        remaining,
        caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
    });
    
    actor.eval.env = caller_env;
    actor.eval.expr = first; // Evaluate first argument
    
    MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)
}
```

</details>

## 5. Left-to-Right Argument Evaluation

Each argument evaluation returns here. We strictly advance one argument at a time, preserving the unevaluated suffix.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 29 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn resume_call_argument(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    function: FunctionValue,
    mut evaluated: Vec<Value>,
    mut remaining: Vec<Expr>,
    caller_env: Environment,
    value: Value,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let arg_index = evaluated.len();
    evaluated.push(value);

    if remaining.is_empty() {
        return apply_function(actor, function, evaluated);
    }

    let next = remaining.remove(0);
    
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::CallArgument {
        function,
        evaluated,
        remaining,
        caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
    });
    
    actor.eval.env = caller_env;
    actor.eval.expr = next;
    
    MachineEvent::EndArgument(arg_index) // Followed immediately by BeginArgument(arg_index + 1) in next step
}
```

</details>

## 6. Function Application (Lexical Scope Enforcement)

This is the critical boundary where lexical scoping is enforced. We extend the *closure's* captured environment, not the caller's.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 18 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn apply_function(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    function: FunctionValue,
    arguments: Vec<Value>,
) -> MachineEvent {
    // Start with the LEXICAL environment captured at lambda creation
    let mut env = function.env.clone();
    
    // Extend it with the evaluated arguments
    for (param, argument) in function.params.into_iter().zip(arguments.into_iter()) {
        env = env.extend(param, argument);
    }
    
    actor.eval.env = env;
    actor.eval.expr = *function.body;
    
    MachineEvent::ApplyFunction
}
```

</details>

## 7. Independent Reference Model (No Production Dependencies)

The reference model must independently implement these rules to serve as a valid oracle.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 73 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub mod reference {
    // ... (previous RefState and reference_step) ...

    fn reference_resume_frame(state: &mut RefState, frame: Frame, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
        match frame {
            // ... (Let, Seq, If) ...
            Frame::CallFunction { args, env } => {
                let function = match value {
                    Value::Function(f) => f,
                    _ => {
                        state.outcome = RefOutcome::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Function", actual: "non-function" });
                        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Function", actual: "non-function" });
                    }
                };

                if function.params.len() != args.len() {
                    let fault = Fault::ArityMismatch { expected: function.params.len(), actual: args.len() };
                    state.outcome = RefOutcome::Fault(fault.clone());
                    return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
                }

                if args.is_empty() {
                    return reference_apply(state, function, Vec::new());
                }

                let mut remaining = args;
                let first = remaining.remove(0);

                state.kont.push(Frame::CallArgument {
                    function,
                    evaluated: Vec::new(),
                    remaining,
                    caller_env: env.clone(),
                });
                
                state.env = env;
                state.expr = first;
                MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)
            }
            Frame::CallArgument { function, mut evaluated, mut remaining, caller_env } => {
                evaluated.push(value);
                if remaining.is_empty() {
                    return reference_apply(state, function, evaluated);
                }
                
                let next = remaining.remove(0);
                let arg_index = evaluated.len() - 1;
                
                state.kont.push(Frame::CallArgument {
                    function,
                    evaluated,
                    remaining,
                    caller_env: caller_env.clone(),
                });
                
                state.env = caller_env;
                state.expr = next;
                MachineEvent::EndArgument(arg_index) // Next step will be BeginArgument
            }
            _ => { /* ... */ }
        }
    }

    fn reference_apply(state: &mut RefState, function: FunctionValue, arguments: Vec<Value>) -> MachineEvent {
        let mut env = function.env.clone(); // LEXICAL CAPTURE
        for (param, argument) in function.params.into_iter().zip(arguments) {
            env = env.extend(param, argument);
        }
        state.env = env;
        state.expr = *function.body;
        MachineEvent::ApplyFunction
    }
}
```

</details>

```rust
        let expr = Expr::Let {

        let mut state = reference::RefState::new(expr, Environment::empty());
        let (_, trace) = run_reference(state, 100_000);

        let mut last_arg_index = -1;
        for event in trace {
            if let MachineEvent::BeginArgument(idx) = event {
                prop_assert!(idx as i32 > last_arg_index, "Arguments must evaluate in strictly increasing index order");
                last_arg_index = idx as i32;

    // 3. Arity Mismatch Prevents Argument Evaluation
    #[test]
    fn arity_mismatch_faults_before_argument_evaluation(
        func_expr in arb_lambda_expr_with_arity(2),
        bad_arg in arb_observable_expr(),
    ) {
        // Call a 2-arg function with 1 arg
        let expr = Expr::Call {
            function: Box::new(func_expr),
            args: vec![bad_arg],
        };

        let mut state = reference::RefState::new(expr, Environment::empty());
        let (_, trace) = run_reference(state, 100);

        // The trace should contain EnterCall, then Fault(ArityMismatch)
        // It must NOT contain BeginArgument(0) or any evaluation of bad_arg
        let has_arity_fault = trace.iter().any(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::ArityMismatch { .. })));
        let has_arg_eval = trace.iter().any(|e| matches!(e, MachineEvent::BeginArgument(0)));

        prop_assert!(has_arity_fault);
        prop_assert!(!has_arg_eval);
    }

            remaining: remaining.clone(),
```

## 9. The Progression to Phase 11

With Phase 10 frozen, the pure CEK machine is now observationally equivalent to the reference model across the full spectrum of lexical scoping, deterministic application, and continuation management. 

The architectural guardrails are set:
1. `Expr::Value` flows through `continue_with_value`.
2. Arity is checked before side effects.

**Next Step: Phase 11 — `Attenuate`**

This is the perfect, minimal bridge to the capability system. `Attenuate` does not touch the host, does not consume external-effect budgets, and does not spawn actors. It purely interacts with the `CapabilityKernel` to derive a new, strictly weaker `CapRef`, which is then passed to the continuation. 

This allows us to test the evaluator/kernel boundary in complete isolation before introducing the complexity of `Request`, `Budget`, and `HostExecutor` in Phase 12.

## [27] CHATGPT (gpt-5-6)

Yes. Phase 11 should now be frozen as the **capability-boundary phase**, but I would make one important semantic correction to the proposed design:

> `Attenuate` should not mutate the caller environment and then evaluate the body permanently in that environment.

Instead, treat attenuation like a lexical binding construct:

\[
\operatorname{attenuate}\;c\;\text{with}\;C\;\text{in}\;body
\]

evaluates `c`, derives a child capability, and evaluates `body` in an environment extended with that child. When `body` returns, the enclosing environment is restored by the continuation frame.

That makes attenuation compositional and gives us a very clean invariant.

# Phase 11 — Attenuate

## 1. Frozen semantics

For:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Attenuate(capability, constraint, body)
```

</details>

the machine performs:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 11 lines</strong></summary>

```text
evaluate capability
        ↓
require Value::Capability(parent)
        ↓
CapabilityKernel::derive(parent, constraint)
        ↓
child CapRef
        ↓
evaluate body with capability binding
        ↓
restore enclosing environment
```

</details>

Semantically:

\[
\langle
\operatorname{attenuate}(c,C,b),
\rho,K,\kappa
\rangle
\]

first evaluates \(c\):

\[
\langle c,\rho,K',\kappa\rangle
\Downarrow CapRef(p)
\]

then:

\[
child=derive(\kappa,p,C)
\]

and evaluates:

\[
b
\]

under an environment containing the derived capability.

The fundamental security invariant is:

\[
\boxed{
child \preceq parent
}
\]

where `≼` is the authority partial order established in the capability algebra.

The evaluator sees only:

</details>

It must **not** be able to inspect:

So the evaluator/kernel interface remains:


The `Authority` itself remains entirely inside the kernel.

This preserves the architectural statement:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Evaluator knows references; Kernel knows authority.}
}

# 5. Capability value validation

When the capability expression returns:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust

```

</details>

the evaluator invokes the kernel.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 46 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn resume_attenuate(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    kernel: &mut CapabilityKernel,
    frame: Frame,
    value: Value,
    now: LogicalTime,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::Attenuate {
        name,
        body,
        env,
    } = frame else {
        unreachable!("resume_attenuate called with wrong frame");
    };

    let parent = match value {
        Value::Capability(cap) => cap,

        _ => {
            let fault = Fault::TypeError {
                expected: "Capability",
                actual: "non-capability",
            };

            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
        }
    };

    match kernel.derive(parent, /* constraint */, now) {
        Ok(child) => {
            actor.eval.env = env.extend(name, Value::Capability(child));
            actor.eval.expr = body;

            MachineEvent::DeriveCapability
        }

        Err(error) => {
            let fault = Fault::Capability(error);

            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());

            MachineEvent::Fault(fault)
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

The exact ownership of `constraint` should be settled in the frame:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
Frame::Attenuate {
    name: Symbol,
    constraint: Constraint,
    body: Expr,
    env: Environment,
}
```

</details>

That is the better version, because the continuation then contains **everything required to resume**.

This satisfies the continuation completeness invariant:

+

\Rightarrow

# 7. Capability derivation must be atomic from the evaluator's perspective

The evaluator should never do:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
validate(parent)
derive(parent)
validate(child)
```

</details>

as three independently observable semantic operations.

The kernel API should make derivation one atomic operation:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub fn derive(
    &mut self,
    parent: CapRef,
    constraint: Constraint,
    now: LogicalTime,
) -> Result<CapRef, CapabilityError>
```

</details>

Internally:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```text
validate parent
       ↓
validate lifetime/revocation
       ↓
intersect authority
       ↓
allocate generation-safe child
       ↓
return CapRef
```

</details>

This prevents an evaluator-level time-of-check/time-of-use gap.

---

# 8. Most important security property

The evaluator itself does **not** prove attenuation.

The kernel proves:

\[
\boxed{
derive(A,C)\preceq A
}
\]

The evaluator only establishes:

\[
Value::Capability(p)
\rightarrow
kernel.derive(p,C)
\rightarrow
Value::Capability(child)
\]

Therefore the combined property is:

\[
\boxed{
Evaluator\;produces\;child
\Rightarrow
child=derive(parent,C)
}
\]

and the kernel supplies:

\[
\boxed{
derive(parent,C)\preceq parent
}
\]

Together:

\[
\boxed{
Evaluator\;cannot\;create\;authority\;stronger\;than\;the\;input\;authority
}
\]

# 9. Capability differential testing needs a second oracle

For Phase 11, the reference machine should **not** instantiate the production `CapabilityKernel`.

Otherwise we'd recreate the exact oracle problem we avoided with CEK.

Create a tiny reference capability model:

<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 12 lines</strong></summary>

Then independently implement:

```rust
fn reference_derive(
    authority: &RefAuthority,
    constraint: &Constraint,
    now: LogicalTime,

```

</details>

using the mathematical intersection rules.

The production kernel's observable result can then be compared with the reference authority **through a controlled test-only projection**, not by giving the evaluator access to authority internals.

# 10. Critical distinction: evaluator test vs kernel test

There are actually two different properties.

### Kernel property

\[
derive(A,C)\preceq A
\]

Test this directly against the independent algebraic model.

### Evaluator property

\[
Attenuate(p,C,b)
\]

must:

1. evaluate `p`;
2. reject non-capabilities;
3. call derivation exactly once;
4. pass the returned child to `b`;
5. preserve the enclosing environment;
6. preserve deterministic continuation behavior;
7. produce no host effect.

These should be separate test suites.

---

# 15. Attenuation must preserve the enclosing environment

Consider:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
let x = 10 in
  attenuate cap as c under C in
    x
```

</details>

The body must still see `x`.

And after completion:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
let x = 10 in
  seq(
    attenuate cap as c under C in unit,
    x
  )
```

</details>

must resolve `x` from the outer environment.

That gives us:

\[
\boxed{
Env_{after(body)} = Env_{before(attenuate)}
}
\]

for the enclosing continuation.

This is exactly why the `Attenuate` frame must store `env`.

---

# 16. Capability attenuation itself gets algebraic properties

Independent of CEK:

### Identity

If the constraint is the top/no-op constraint:

\[
derive(A,\top)=A
\]

modulo capability identity/generation semantics.

### Idempotence

Applying the same attenuation twice:

\[
derive(derive(A,C),C)
\preceq
derive(A,C)
\]

and under ordinary intersection semantics:

\[
derive(derive(A,C),C)
=
derive(A,C)
\]

at the authority level.

### Commutativity

For compatible constraints:

\[
derive(derive(A,C_1),C_2)
=
derive(derive(A,C_2),C_1)
\]

at the authority-semantics level.

### Monotonicity

If:

\[
C_1\preceq C_2
\]

then:

\[
derive(A,C_1)\preceq derive(A,C_2)
\]

These are excellent property-test targets because they exercise the actual capability algebra rather than merely checking implementation plumbing.

---

# 17. Revocation must already be visible to attenuation

Because `derive` validates the parent at an explicit logical time:

\[
Valid(parent,t)
\]

is required before derivation.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\neg Valid(parent,t)
\Rightarrow
derive(parent,C,t)=Err
}
\]

This catches an important security bug: **attenuation must not become a way of laundering a revoked authority into a fresh capability.**

In particular:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```text
live parent
   ↓
derive child
   ↓
revoke parent
   ↓
child invalid
```

</details>

must continue to hold because descendant validity walks the ancestor chain.

---

# 18. No budget consumption beyond ordinary computation

Phase 11 is deliberately not an effect operation.

So attenuation should not consume:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
I/O
duration attributable to host effects
memory reservation
concurrency slots
```

</details>

It may consume the normal evaluator fuel for executing the instruction.

The clean rule is:

\[
\boxed{
Attenuate \notin ExternalEffect
}
\]

and therefore:

\[
\boxed{
Attenuate
\not\Rightarrow
HostExecutor
}
\]

This becomes an architectural test, not merely a runtime assertion.

---

# Phase 11 acceptance gate

| Property | Verification |
|---|---|
| Capability expression evaluated first | Differential trace |
| Exactly one `derive` call | Mock-kernel property |
| Correct parent `CapRef` | Mock-kernel property |
| Exact constraint forwarded | Mock-kernel property |
| Explicit logical time forwarded | Mock-kernel property |
| Non-capability rejected | Property |
| Derivation failure prevents body | Property |
| Derived capability bound correctly | Differential |
| Lexical environment preserved | Differential |
| Enclosing environment restored | Differential |
| Child authority ≤ parent authority | Independent kernel algebra |
| Revoked parent cannot derive | Kernel property |
| Expired parent cannot derive | Kernel property |
| Descendant revocation preserved | Kernel property |
| No host invocation | Structural + negative test |
| No external-effect budget consumption | Accounting property |
| Continuation serialization | Round-trip |
| Resume after serialization | Differential |
| Production CEK does not inspect authority | Module/API boundary |

## The resulting security chain

Once Phase 11 passes, we have a particularly clean composition:

\[
\boxed{
Value::Capability(p)
\xrightarrow{\text{validated evaluator transition}}
derive(p,C)
\xrightarrow{\text{kernel}}
child
}
\]

with:

\[
\boxed{
child\preceq p
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
Attenuate\;cannot\;produce\;an\;authority\;stronger\;than\;its\;input
}
\]

But importantly, **Phase 11 still cannot cause an external effect**.

That leaves the next boundary exceptionally sharp:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Phase 11: Attenuate}
\rightarrow
\text{Phase 12: Request}
}
\]

Phase 12 is where we must finally compose **capability authorization + resource ceilings + runtime budget + deadline + host policy + deterministic effect IDs + `Pending` state**, and that is where the transactional `EffectIssued` / `EffectCompleted` protocol becomes mandatory.

---

## [28] USER

This is a masterful refinement. By modeling `Attenuate` as a lexical binding construct (`attenuate cap as child under C in body`), we achieve perfect symmetry with `Let`, guaranteeing environment restoration and compositional semantics. Furthermore, your insistence on using a **Mock Kernel** for the CEK trace tests, while testing the **Reference Algebra** independently, completely eliminates the oracle problem. We are no longer testing if the implementation matches itself; we are testing if the evaluator correctly orchestrates the kernel's API, and if the kernel correctly implements the mathematical algebra.

Below is the **Phase 11 Frozen Implementation and Verification Blueprint**, strictly adhering to your 20-point specification.

---

### 1. Updated AST and Continuation Frames

We explicitly bind the derived capability to a `name` in the body's environment.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 29 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Expr {
    // ... (Value, Var, Let, Seq, If, Lambda, Call)
    Attenuate {
        capability: Box<Expr>,
        name: Symbol,          // Explicit binding name
        constraint: Constraint,
        body: Box<Expr>,
    },
    // ... (Request, Spawn, Send, Receive)
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Frame {
    // ... (LetValue, Seq, If, CallFunction, CallArgument)
    Attenuate {
        name: Symbol,
        constraint: Constraint,
        body: Expr,
        env: Environment,
    },
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MachineEvent {
    // ... (Previous events)
    EnterAttenuate,
    DeriveCapability,
}
```

</details>

### 2. The Evaluator Transitions (Phase 11)

The evaluator treats `Attenuate` purely as a control-flow and environment-manipulation construct. It knows nothing of authority semantics.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 60 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
// Entry: Evaluate the capability expression first
fn enter_attenuate(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    capability: Expr,
    name: Symbol,
    constraint: Constraint,
    body: Expr,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let env = actor.eval.env.clone();
    
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::Attenuate {
        name,
        constraint,
        body,
        env,
    });
    
    actor.eval.expr = capability;
    MachineEvent::EnterAttenuate
}

// Resumption: Called by `continue_with_value` when the capability expression yields a Value
fn resume_attenuate<K: CapabilityKernelView>(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    kernel: &mut K,
    frame: Frame,
    value: Value,
    now: LogicalTime,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::Attenuate { name, constraint, body, env } = frame else {
        unreachable!("resume_attenuate called with wrong frame");
    };

    let parent = match value {
        Value::Capability(cap) => cap,
        _ => {
            let fault = Fault::TypeError {
                expected: "Capability",
                actual: "non-capability",
            };
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
        }
    };

    // ATOMIC DERIVATION: The kernel handles validation, intersection, and allocation.
    match kernel.derive(parent, &constraint, now) {
        Ok(child) => {
            // Extend the SAVED environment with the new child capability
            actor.eval.env = env.extend(name, Value::Capability(child));
            actor.eval.expr = body;
            MachineEvent::DeriveCapability
        }
        Err(error) => {
            let fault = Fault::CapabilityError(error);
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            MachineEvent::Fault(fault)
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

### 3. The Capability Kernel Interface & Mock

We define a narrow trait. The production kernel implements this, and tests use a mock.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 47 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CapabilityError {
    Revoked,
    Expired,
    InvalidConstraint,
    // ...
}

pub trait CapabilityKernelView {
    fn derive(
        &mut self,
        parent: CapRef,
        constraint: &Constraint,
        now: LogicalTime,
    ) -> Result<CapRef, CapabilityError>;
}

// Mock Kernel for Evaluator Differential Tests
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct MockKernel {
    pub calls: Vec<DeriveCall>,
    pub results: std::collections::VecDeque<Result<CapRef, CapabilityError>>,
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct DeriveCall {
    pub parent: CapRef,
    pub constraint: Constraint,
    pub now: LogicalTime,
}

impl MockKernel {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self { calls: Vec::new(), results: std::collections::VecDeque::new() }
    }
    
    pub fn push_result(&mut self, result: Result<CapRef, CapabilityError>) {
        self.results.push_back(result);
    }
}

impl CapabilityKernelView for MockKernel {
    fn derive(&mut self, parent: CapRef, constraint: &Constraint, now: LogicalTime) -> Result<CapRef, CapabilityError> {
        self.calls.push(DeriveCall { parent, constraint: constraint.clone(), now });
        self.results.pop_front().unwrap_or(Err(CapabilityError::InvalidConstraint))
    }
}
```

</details>

```rust
proptest! {

        parent_cap in arb_cap_ref(),

        constraint in arb_constraint(),

    ) {

        kernel.push_result(Err(CapabilityError::Revoked));

        let expr = Expr::Attenuate {

            name: Symbol(1),
            constraint,
            body: Box::new(Expr::Value(Value::Unit)), // This should never be evaluated
        };

        let c = Symbol(2);
        let mut kernel = MockKernel::new();

        // let x = outer_val in attenuate cap as c under C in x
        let expr = Expr::Let {
            name: x,

        prop_assert!(matches!(result, Outcome::Halted(_) | Outcome::Fault(_)));
```

### 5. The Independent Reference Capability Algebra (Kernel Verification)

Separately from the CEK machine, we verify the kernel's mathematical soundness.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 45 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
// Reference Model (Pure Math)
pub fn reference_derive(
    authority: &RefAuthority,
    constraint: &RefConstraint,
    now: LogicalTime,
) -> Result<RefAuthority, RefCapabilityError> {
    if !reference_is_valid(authority, now) {
        return Err(RefCapabilityError::ExpiredOrRevoked);
    }
    
    // Pure intersection semantics
    Ok(RefAuthority {
        operations: intersect_ops(&authority.operations, &constraint.operations),
        scope: intersect_scope(&authority.scope, &constraint.scope),
        // ... params, resources, lifetime intersection
    })
}

proptest! {
    // Kernel Property: Attenuation Soundness
    #[test]
    fn reference_derive_is_always_less_or_equal(
        authority in arb_ref_authority(),
        constraint in arb_ref_constraint(),
        now in arb_logical_time(),
    ) {
        if let Ok(derived) = reference_derive(&authority, &constraint, now) {
            prop_assert!(derived.leq(&authority), "Derived authority must be <= parent authority");
        }
    }

    // Kernel Property: Idempotence of Constraint
    #[test]
    fn reference_derive_is_idempotent(
        authority in arb_ref_authority(),
        constraint in arb_ref_constraint(),
        now in arb_logical_time(),
    ) {
        if let Ok(first) = reference_derive(&authority, &constraint, now) {
            if let Ok(second) = reference_derive(&first, &constraint, now) {
                prop_assert_eq!(first, second, "Applying same constraint twice yields identical authority");
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Phase 11 Acceptance Gate Achieved

By structuring the verification this way, we have proven two distinct, vital properties:
1. **Evaluator Correctness**: The CEK machine correctly sequences evaluation, rejects non-capabilities, invokes the kernel *exactly once* with the correct arguments, binds the result lexically, and restores the environment. It does this without ever inspecting authority internals or touching the host.
2. **Kernel Soundness**: The independent reference algebra proves that `derive(A, C) <= A`, ensuring that no matter what the evaluator asks for, the kernel mathematically guarantees attenuation.

### The Path to Phase 12: Request

We have successfully crossed the capability boundary. The evaluator can now safely manipulate and attenuate capabilities. 

**Phase 12 (Request)** is the final, most complex boundary. It is where all previous layers converge:
1. The CEK machine evaluates the `Request` expression (capability, target, params).
2. It constructs a canonical `Effect`.
3. It checks the **Dual Gate**: `kernel.authorize(cap, effect, now)` AND `budget.can_consume(effect.cost)`.
4. It checks `HostPolicyOK`.
5. It allocates a deterministic `EffectId`, consumes/reserves budget, appends `EffectIssued` to the log, and transitions to `ActorStatus::Pending`.
6. The host executes, and `resume_from_receipt` causally validates the `EffectDigest` before resuming the continuation.

Shall we draft the Phase 12 `Request` semantics, establishing the final, fully composed transactional boundary between the deterministic machine and the nondeterministic host?

***

This is the definitive specification for Phase 11. By treating attenuation as a lexical binding construct and enforcing a strict two-track verification architecture (Evaluator + Mock Kernel vs. Production Kernel + Reference Algebra), we completely eliminate the oracle problem and establish a mathematically rigorous capability boundary.

Here is the frozen **Phase 11: Attenuate** blueprint.

# Phase 11: Attenuate (Frozen Capability-Boundary)

## 1. AST and Frame Updates

We explicitly bind the derived capability to a name, making attenuation compositionally identical to `Let` in its environment discipline.

## 2. Evaluator Transitions

The evaluator strictly evaluates the capability expression first, then delegates derivation to the kernel in a single, atomic step.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 55 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn enter_attenuate(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    capability: Expr,
    name: Symbol,
    constraint: Constraint,
    body: Expr,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let env = actor.eval.env.clone();
    
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::Attenuate {
        name,
        constraint,
        body,
        env,
    });
    
    actor.eval.expr = capability;
    MachineEvent::EnterAttenuate
}

fn resume_attenuate(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    kernel: &mut dyn CapabilityKernelView,
    frame: Frame,
    value: Value,
    now: LogicalTime,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::Attenuate { name, constraint, body, env } = frame else {
        unreachable!("resume_attenuate called with wrong frame");
    };

    let parent = match value {
        Value::Capability(cap) => cap,
        _ => {
            let fault = Fault::TypeError { expected: "Capability", actual: "non-capability" };
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
        }
    };

    // ATOMIC DERIVATION: Evaluator does not validate or inspect authority.
    match kernel.derive(parent, &constraint, now) {
        Ok(child) => {
            // Lexical binding of the derived capability
            actor.eval.env = env.extend(name, Value::Capability(child));
            actor.eval.expr = body;
            MachineEvent::DeriveCapability
        }
        Err(error) => {
            let fault = Fault::CapabilityError(error);
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            MachineEvent::Fault(fault)
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

## 3. The Two-Track Verification Architecture

To prevent the implementation from becoming its own oracle, we split verification into two independent axes.

### Track A: Evaluator Control Flow (via Mock Kernel)
The evaluator is parameterized over a narrow trait. The mock kernel records calls and returns pre-configured results, allowing us to prove control flow without exposing authority internals.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 27 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub trait CapabilityKernelView {
    fn derive(
        &mut self,
        parent: CapRef,
        constraint: &Constraint,
        now: LogicalTime,
    ) -> Result<CapRef, CapabilityError>;
}

pub struct MockKernel {
    pub calls: Vec<DeriveCall>,
    pub results: VecDeque<Result<CapRef, CapabilityError>>,
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct DeriveCall {
    pub parent: CapRef,
    pub constraint: Constraint,
    pub now: LogicalTime,
}

impl CapabilityKernelView for MockKernel {
    fn derive(&mut self, parent: CapRef, constraint: &Constraint, now: LogicalTime) -> Result<CapRef, CapabilityError> {
        self.calls.push(DeriveCall { parent, constraint: constraint.clone(), now });
        self.results.pop_front().unwrap_or_else(|| Err(CapabilityError::Invalid))
    }
}
```

</details>

```rust
        value in arb_non_capability_value(),

            name: Symbol(1),
            constraint,
            body: Box::new(Expr::Value(Value::Unit)),
        };

        prop_assert!(matches!(result, Outcome::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Capability", .. })));

            body: Box::new(observable_test_expression()), // Would emit a trace event if evaluated
        };

        let (_, trace) = run_with_kernel_and_trace(expr, &mut kernel);

        prop_assert!(trace_contains_fault(&trace));

        constraint in arb_constraint(),
```
```rust
        now in arb_logical_time(),
```

## Phase 11 Acceptance Gate Achieved

With this structure, we have successfully frozen the capability boundary. The verification is now mathematically rigorous:

1. **Evaluator Control Flow** is proven via the Mock Kernel to evaluate strictly left-to-right, reject non-capabilities, call derivation exactly once, and preserve lexical environments.
2. **Kernel Correctness** is proven via the Reference Algebra to guarantee `derive(A,C) <= A`, enforce revocation, and maintain idempotence.
3. **No Host Leakage** is proven structurally and via negative testing.

The resulting security chain is airtight:
$$ \boxed{ Value::Capability(p) \xrightarrow{\text{evaluator}} derive(p,C) \xrightarrow{\text{kernel}} child \implies child \preceq p } $$

This is the final, most complex boundary. Phase 12 is where we must compose **capability authorization + resource ceilings + runtime budget + deadline + host policy + deterministic effect IDs + `Pending` state**. The transactional `EffectIssued` / `EffectCompleted` protocol becomes mandatory here, and the 14-step authorization sequence will be rigorously enforced.

# Phase 12 — `Request`: Frozen Transactional Effect Boundary

## 1. Semantic shape

The AST remains:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
Expr::Request {
    capability: Box<Expr>,
    operation: Op,
    target: Box<Expr>,
    params: Vec<Expr>,
}
```

</details>

The important semantic distinction is that `Request` has **three evaluation phases**:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 33 lines</strong></summary>

```text
                    deterministic
                         │
                         ▼
             ┌─────────────────────┐
             │ Evaluate capability │
             └──────────┬──────────┘
                        ▼
             ┌─────────────────────┐
             │ Evaluate target     │
             └──────────┬──────────┘
                        ▼
             ┌─────────────────────┐
             │ Evaluate parameters │
             │ left → right        │
             └──────────┬──────────┘
                        ▼
                 canonical Effect
                        │
                  all gates pass
                        │
                        ▼
                 EffectIssued
                        │
                        ▼
                    Pending
                        │
                  host boundary
                        │
                        ▼
                 EffectCompleted
                        │
                        ▼
                 resume CEK
```

</details>

The host is therefore **not part of expression evaluation**. It is an external participant in a machine transition.

---

# 2. Request frame

`Request` needs a continuation frame that explicitly records the partially evaluated request.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 27 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Frame {
    // ...

    RequestCapability {
        operation: Op,
        target: Expr,
        params: Vec<Expr>,
        env: Environment,
    },

    RequestTarget {
        capability: CapRef,
        operation: Op,
        params: Vec<Expr>,
        caller_env: Environment,
    },

    RequestArgument {
        capability: CapRef,
        operation: Op,
        target: Value,
        evaluated: Vec<Value>,
        remaining: Vec<Expr>,
        caller_env: Environment,
    },
}
```

</details>

This gives us the same invariant already established for calls:

\[
|evaluated|+|remaining|=n
\]

for a request containing \(n\) parameters.

More importantly, it prevents a partially evaluated request from being reconstructed implicitly from mutable evaluator state.

---

# 3. Request status

The actor's pending state needs to carry the complete causally relevant request context.

I recommend:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 17 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ActorStatus {
    Running,

    Pending {
        effect_id: EffectId,
        effect: Effect,
        continuation: Continuation,
        reservation: Reserved,
    },

    Blocked(Continuation),

    Halted(Value),

    Fault(Fault),
}
```

</details>

However, there is an important architectural choice here.

If `eval.continuation` remains the canonical continuation location, **do not duplicate it in `Pending`**. Prefer:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 15 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum ActorStatus {
    Running,

    Pending {
        effect_id: EffectId,
        effect: Effect,
        reservation: Reserved,
    },

    Blocked,

    Halted(Value),

    Fault(Fault),
}
```

</details>

The evaluator state remains intact while pending:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
ActorState
 ├── eval
 │    ├── expr
 │    ├── env
 │    └── continuation
 └── status = Pending(...)
```

</details>

This avoids having two potentially divergent continuations.

# 4. Canonical effect identity

Freeze these types now:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust

pub struct EffectId(pub u64);

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct EffectDigest(pub [u8; 32]);
```

</details>

The digest must be computed over a canonical representation of the effect.

Conceptually:

\[
digest(E)=H(canonical(E))
\]

It should include at least:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
operation
target
parameters
capability identity
effect-specific metadata
```

</details>

The exact serialization format should be frozen before implementing replay.

The key property is:

\[
E_1=E_2
\Rightarrow
digest(E_1)=digest(E_2)
\]

and, for canonical serialization:

\[
digest(E_1)=digest(E_2)
\Rightarrow
E_1=E_2
\]

within the supported effect domain.

# 5. Effect structure

I would make the effect explicitly contain its normalized cost:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 8 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Effect {
    pub capability: CapRef,
    pub operation: Op,
    pub target: Target,
    pub params: Params,
    pub cost: EffectCost,
}
```

</details>

With the bookkeeping correction from the earlier phases, freeze:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct EffectCost {
    pub issue: Consumable,
    pub complete: Consumable,
    pub reserve: Reserved,
}
```

</details>

Thus:

\[
cost(E)=
\langle
cost_{issue}(E),
cost_{complete}(E),
reserve(E)
\rangle
\]

This resolves the earlier ambiguity over whether I/O/duration gets charged at request time, completion time, or both.

**Do not charge the same resource twice.**

---

# 6. The fourteen-gate sequence

The request transition should be mechanically implemented in this exact order.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 14 lines</strong></summary>

```text
1. capability expression evaluates
2. target expression evaluates
3. parameters evaluate left → right
4. canonical Effect constructed
5. capability handle validated
6. exact effect authorized by capability
7. capability resource ceiling checked
8. runtime consumable budget checked
9. runtime reservation checked
10. deadline checked
11. host policy checked
12. deterministic EffectId allocated
13. issue budget/reservation committed + EffectIssued logged
14. actor becomes Pending and host receives request
```

</details>

The critical security invariant is:

\[
HostExecute(E)
\Rightarrow
\bigwedge_{i=5}^{11} Gate_i(E)
\land Issued(E)
\]

No host call is legal before step 13.

---

# 7. Evaluating the capability

Entry:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 22 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn enter_request(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    capability: Expr,
    operation: Op,
    target: Expr,
    params: Vec<Expr>,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let env = actor.eval.env.clone();

    actor.eval.continuation.push(
        Frame::RequestCapability {
            operation,
            target,
            params,
            env,
        }
    );

    actor.eval.expr = capability;

    MachineEvent::EnterRequest
}
```

</details>

When the capability expression returns:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 43 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn resume_request_capability(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    frame: Frame,
    value: Value,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::RequestCapability {
        operation,
        target,
        params,
        env,
    } = frame else {
        unreachable!();
    };

    let capability = match value {
        Value::Capability(cap) => cap,

        _ => {
            let fault = Fault::TypeError {
                expected: "Capability",
                actual: "non-capability",
            };

            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(fault.clone());
            return MachineEvent::Fault(fault);
        }
    };

    actor.eval.env = env.clone();

    actor.eval.continuation.push(
        Frame::RequestTarget {
            capability,
            operation,
            params,
            caller_env: env,
        }
    );

    actor.eval.expr = target;

    MachineEvent::BeginRequestTarget
}
```

</details>

This guarantees that an invalid capability expression never evaluates the target or parameters.

---

# 8. Target evaluation

When the target evaluates:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 29 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn resume_request_target(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    frame: Frame,
    target: Value,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::RequestTarget {
        capability,
        operation,
        params,
        caller_env,
    } = frame else {
        unreachable!();
    };

    actor.eval.env = caller_env.clone();

    actor.eval.continuation.push(
        Frame::RequestArgument {
            capability,
            operation,
            target,
            evaluated: Vec::new(),
            remaining: params,
            caller_env,
        }
    );

    begin_next_request_argument(actor)
}
```

</details>

# 9. Left-to-right parameter evaluation

The transition should explicitly move one argument at a time.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 54 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn begin_next_request_argument(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let frame = actor.eval.continuation.pop().expect("request frame");

    let Frame::RequestArgument {
        capability,
        operation,
        target,
        mut evaluated,
        mut remaining,
        caller_env,
    } = frame else {
        unreachable!();
    };

    match remaining.is_empty() {
        true => {
            actor.eval.continuation.push(
                Frame::RequestArgument {
                    capability,
                    operation,
                    target,
                    evaluated,
                    remaining,
                    caller_env,
                }
            );

            finalize_request(actor)
        }

        false => {
            let expr = remaining.remove(0);

            actor.eval.continuation.push(
                Frame::RequestArgument {
                    capability,
                    operation,
                    target,
                    evaluated,
                    remaining,
                    caller_env,
                }
            );

            actor.eval.expr = expr;

            MachineEvent::BeginRequestArgument(
                // index is derivable from evaluated count
            )
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

The actual implementation can be cleaner than this, but the semantic invariant should be:

\[
\boxed{
\text{exactly one argument is removed from remaining per evaluation}
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
\text{arguments are evaluated strictly left-to-right}
}
\]

---

# 10. Canonicalization

Once all values are available:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
capability
operation
target
params[]
```

</details>

the evaluator constructs a canonical effect.

This is an important boundary.

The evaluator may construct **data describing the requested effect**, but it must not decide whether that effect is permitted.

Conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
let effect = canonicalize_effect(
    capability,
    operation,
    target,
    evaluated_params,
)?;
```

</details>

`canonicalize_effect` may perform:

- type validation,
- normalization,
- canonical serialization preparation,
- cost calculation.

It must **not**:

- bypass capability authorization,
- consult host state,
- execute the effect,
- mutate external state.
