# 11. Capability authorization

Now the evaluator enters the security kernel:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
kernel.authorize(
    capability,
    &effect,
    now,
)?;
```

</details>

The authorization predicate remains:

\[
Authorized(A,E,t)
\iff
\begin{aligned}
&E.op\in O_A\\
{}\land{}&
E.target\in\llbracket A_{E.op}.S\rrbracket\\
{}\land{}&
A_{E.op}.Q(E.params)\\
{}\land{}&
cost(E)\le R_A\\
{}\land{}&
t\in A_{E.op}.T
\end{aligned}
\]

The evaluator must not reproduce these checks.

That would recreate the exact oracle/authority leakage problem we eliminated in Phase 11.

---

# 12. Capability ceiling versus runtime budget

The two gates remain independent:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Capability ceiling
        +
Runtime budget
        ↓
      allowed
```

</details>

Formally:

\[
cost(E)\le R_A
\]

and:

\[
cost(E)\le B_{available}
\]

must both hold.

A capability may authorize an effect that the actor's current budget cannot afford.

Conversely, an actor may have sufficient budget for an effect that its capability does not authorize.

Neither implies the other.

---

# 13. Budget accounting

At issue time, consume only the issue portion:

\[
C' = C-cost_{issue}(E)
\]

and reserve:

\[
R'=R-reserve(E)
\]

using checked arithmetic.

Conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
let new_consumable =
    budget.consumable.checked_sub(effect.cost.issue)
        .ok_or(Fault::BudgetExhausted)?;

let new_reserved =
    budget.reserved.checked_sub(effect.cost.reserve)
        .ok_or(Fault::BudgetExhausted)?;
```

</details>

No saturating arithmetic.

No wrapping arithmetic.

No implicit conversion from overflow into success.

If arithmetic fails, the request does not cross the host boundary.

---

# 14. Deadline

Freeze deadline semantics explicitly:

\[
t_{now}\le W
\]

before issuance.

I recommend also checking the predicted completion requirement if the effect declares a duration:

\[
t_{now}+\Delta t_{expected}\le W
\]

**only if** the effect model actually has a trustworthy declared duration bound.

Otherwise, only enforce the request-time deadline and treat an overlong host completion as a completion-time deadline violation.

Do not pretend an untrusted host duration prediction is deterministic.

---

# 15. Host policy

Host policy is the final host-side authorization gate before issuance:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
host_policy.check(&effect)
```

</details>

For example:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub trait HostPolicy {
    fn authorize(
        &self,
        effect: &Effect,
    ) -> Result<(), HostPolicyError>;
}
```

</details>

This is deliberately separate from the capability kernel.

The security architecture therefore has three distinct authorities:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Capability authority
        ↓
Runtime resource authority
        ↓
Host deployment policy
```

</details>

All three must agree.

---

# 16. Deterministic effect allocation

Only after all gates succeed:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
let effect_id = effect_ids.allocate();
```

</details>

The allocator is part of deterministic machine state:

\[
N_h\in G
\]

with:

\[
N_h'=N_h+1
\]

No random UUID.

No host-generated ID.

No wall-clock timestamp.

No pointer address.

This makes the effect identity replayable.

---

# 17. Transactional issuance

This is the most important part of Phase 12.

Do **not** perform:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
debit budget
log issued
host execute
```

</details>

as unrelated mutations.

The machine must conceptually perform one atomic transition:

\[
\boxed{
State
\rightarrow
State'
+
EffectIssued
+
EffectRequest
}
\]

where `State'` already contains the committed accounting and `Pending` state.

The event:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum MachineEvent {
    // ...

    EffectIssued {
        id: EffectId,
        digest: EffectDigest,
    },

    EffectCompleted {
        id: EffectId,
        digest: EffectDigest,
    },
}
```

</details>

should causally correspond to the pending request.

---

# 18. EffectIssued record

I recommend making the persisted event richer than merely `(id, digest)`:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 8 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct EffectIssued {
    pub id: EffectId,
    pub actor: ActorId,
    pub effect_digest: EffectDigest,
    pub logical_time: LogicalTime,
    pub issue_cost: Consumable,
    pub reservation: Reserved,
}
```

</details>

This makes replay/accounting reconstruction substantially stronger.

The invariant becomes:

\[
\boxed{
EffectIssued(id,E)
\Rightarrow
budget\_transition(E)
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
Pending(id)
\iff
\text{uncompleted issued effect }id
}
\]

subject to the machine's fault/recovery semantics.

---

# 19. Pending transition

After issuance:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
actor.status = ActorStatus::Pending {
    effect_id,
    effect: effect.clone(),
    reservation: effect.cost.reserve,
};
```

</details>

The machine then yields:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
EffectRequest {
    id: effect_id,
    effect,
    cap: capability,
}
```

</details>

to the host adapter.

The crucial architectural rule:

> **The CEK machine does not call `HostExecutor::execute` directly as part of expression reduction.**

Instead:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 11 lines</strong></summary>

```text
CEK
 ↓
EffectRequest
 ↓
scheduler / host adapter
 ↓
HostExecutor
 ↓
EffectReceipt
 ↓
machine resume
```

</details>

This keeps the host boundary explicit.

---

# 20. Receipt protocol

The receipt must contain:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct EffectReceipt {
    pub id: EffectId,
    pub effect_digest: EffectDigest,
    pub result: Result<Value, HostFault>,
}
```

</details>

On receipt:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn resume_from_receipt(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    receipt: EffectReceipt,
    now: LogicalTime,
) -> MachineEvent
```

</details>

first verify:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
actor is Pending
receipt.id == pending.effect_id
receipt.effect_digest == digest(pending.effect)
```

</details>

Only then may the result influence the machine.

---

# 21. Causal receipt validation

The core rule is:

\[
\boxed{
AcceptReceipt(r)
\iff
r.id=id_{pending}
\land
r.digest=digest(E_{pending})
}
\]

A matching ID with a mismatching digest is **not** sufficient.

That prevents a stale or substituted receipt from being attached to the wrong effect.

Failure:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
Fault::ReplayCorruption
```

</details>

and critically:

> **Do not resume the continuation.**

---

# 22. Completion accounting

At successful causal validation, charge completion cost:

\[
C'=C-cost_{complete}(E)
\]

Then release reservations:

\[
R'=R-reserve(E)
\]

This gives the clean lifecycle:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```text
ISSUE
  │
  ├── consume issue cost
  └── reserve resources
       │
       ▼
    PENDING
       │
       ▼
 COMPLETE
  │
  ├── consume completion cost
  └── release reservation
```

</details>

This resolves the earlier double-charge ambiguity.

---

# 23. Completion event

Only after successful validation and accounting:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
MachineEvent::EffectCompleted {
    id: receipt.id,
    digest: receipt.effect_digest,
}
```

</details>

Then:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
actor.status = ActorStatus::Running;
```

</details>

and:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
continue_with_value(actor, result)
```

</details>

or fault according to the host result semantics.

A host failure is a **machine-visible result/fault**, not necessarily replay corruption.

For example:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
File not found
permission denied
connection refused
process exited nonzero
```

</details>

may be legitimate nondeterministic host outcomes and therefore belong in the receipt.

A mismatched receipt is fundamentally different:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
wrong effect ID
wrong effect digest
```

</details>

which indicates a protocol/replay integrity failure.

---

# 24. ReplayHost

Replay must never execute the external effect again.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct ReplayHost {
    receipts: ReceiptLog,
}
```

</details>

Its behavior is conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 11 lines</strong></summary>

```text
EffectRequest(id, digest)
        │
        ▼
lookup recorded receipt
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   │         │
 found     missing
   │         │
   ▼         ▼
receipt   ReplayCorruption
```

</details>

Therefore:

\[
ReplayHost \not\rightarrow ExternalWorld
\]

and:

\[
Replay(E)
\rightarrow
RecordedReceipt(E)
\]

rather than:

\[
Replay(E)\rightarrow HostExecute(E)
\]

---

# 25. The critical negative property

This should become a foundational security test:

\[
\boxed{
\neg AllGatesPass(E)
\Rightarrow
HostExecutor.execute(E)\text{ is never called}
}
\]

Not merely "usually not called."

Every denial path must prove it.

---

# 26. Phase 12 fault taxonomy

I would freeze something close to:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 35 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum Fault {
    // existing

    UnboundVariable(Symbol),

    TypeError {
        expected: &'static str,
        actual: &'static str,
    },

    ArityMismatch {
        expected: usize,
        actual: usize,
    },

    Capability(CapabilityError),

    BudgetExhausted,

    DeadlineExceeded,

    HostPolicyDenied(HostPolicyError),

    EffectCanonicalization(EffectError),

    Host(HostFault),

    ReplayCorruption,

    InvalidReceipt,

    PendingEffectMismatch,

    ArithmeticOverflow,
}
```

</details>

Do not collapse all of these into one generic "request denied" error. The distinction is valuable for deterministic reasoning and diagnostics.

---

# 27. Denial precedence

Freeze the ordering.

I recommend:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
1. capability validity
2. capability authorization
3. capability resource ceiling
4. runtime budget
5. deadline
6. host policy
```

</details>

Why capability first?

Because an unauthorized effect should never be evaluated as merely a resource shortage.

The security interpretation is:

\[
\neg Authorized(E)
\Rightarrow
\text{the machine has no authority to perform }E
\]

Budget failure is operational, not authoritative.

---

# 28. Request property suite

Phase 12 needs substantially more than a single differential test.

## Track A — CEK control flow

### Property 1 — capability evaluated first

Generate observable expressions:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
capability → marker A
target     → marker B
arg0       → marker C
arg1       → marker D
```

</details>

Assert:

\[
A<B<C<D
\]

in the trace.

---

### Property 2 — invalid capability short-circuits

For:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Request(non_capability, target, args)
```

</details>

assert:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
derive/authorize calls = 0
target evaluation = 0
argument evaluation = 0
host calls = 0
```

</details>

---

### Property 3 — target precedes parameters

For valid capability:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
target → marker T
arg0   → marker A
arg1   → marker B
```

</details>

assert:

\[
T<A<B
\]

---

### Property 4 — parameters are left-to-right

For \(n\) arguments:

\[
trace = BeginArgument(0),EndArgument(0),
        BeginArgument(1),EndArgument(1),\ldots
\]

or whatever exact frozen event protocol is selected.

---

### Property 5 — canonical effect correctness

Generate:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
cap
operation
target
params
```

</details>

and assert that the resulting `Effect` contains exactly those values after canonicalization.

This is particularly important because the effect is the object ultimately authorized by the kernel.

---

# 29. Track B — kernel authorization

Use a mock authorization kernel analogous to Phase 11:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct MockAuthorizationKernel {
    pub calls: Vec<AuthorizeCall>,
    pub result: Result<(), CapabilityError>,
}
```

</details>

Record:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct AuthorizeCall {
    pub capability: CapRef,
    pub effect: Effect,
    pub now: LogicalTime,
}
```

</details>

Then prove:

\[
\#authorizeCalls=1
\]

and:

\[
authorizeCall.capability=cap
\]

\[
authorizeCall.effect=canonicalEffect
\]

\[
authorizeCall.now=t
\]

The evaluator must not independently inspect authority semantics.

---

# 30. Track C — gate short-circuit properties

For each gate, install later-stage spies that would panic if reached.

For example:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 11 lines</strong></summary>

```text
CapabilityDenied
      ↓
budget spy must remain untouched
      ↓
host-policy spy untouched
      ↓
effect allocator untouched
      ↓
event log unchanged
      ↓
host untouched
```

</details>

Then independently:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```text
BudgetDenied
      ↓
host-policy untouched
      ↓
effect allocator untouched
      ↓
log unchanged
      ↓
host untouched
```

</details>

And:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
HostPolicyDenied
      ↓
effect is never issued
      ↓
host never executes
```

</details>

This gives us a **negative proof matrix**, rather than testing only successful requests.

---

# 31. Transactional issuance property

This is one of the strongest Phase 12 tests.

For every denied request:

\[
\boxed{
budget' = budget
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
log'=log
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
N_h'=N_h
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
status'\ne Pending
}
\]

In other words:

> **Failed authorization does not consume an effect ID, does not debit the budget, does not reserve resources, and does not append `EffectIssued`.**

That is an extremely useful invariant.

---

# 32. Successful issuance property

Conversely, for an accepted request:

\[
N_h'=N_h+1
\]

\[
C'=C-cost_{issue}(E)
\]

\[
R'=R-reserve(E)
\]

\[
log'=log\mathbin{\|}EffectIssued
\]

and:

\[
status'=Pending(id,E,\ldots)
\]

all in the same logical transition.

---

# 33. Exactly-once host request

For every issued effect:

\[
\boxed{
\#HostRequest(id)=1
}
\]

The machine must not accidentally resubmit the same pending request when:

- scheduler runs again,
- actor is descheduled,
- continuation is serialized,
- unrelated actor executes,
- receipt is delayed.

This is where the explicit `Pending` state earns its keep.

---

# 34. Receipt properties

For a valid receipt:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Pending(id, E)
receipt(id, digest(E))
```

</details>

assert:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
→ completion accounting
→ EffectCompleted
→ Running
→ continuation resumes exactly once
```

</details>

For an invalid digest:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Pending(id, E)
receipt(id, digest(E2))
```

</details>

assert:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
→ ReplayCorruption
→ continuation does not resume
→ no completion event
→ no resource release
```

</details>

The exact recovery policy can later define whether the actor remains faulted or the entire machine enters a replay-integrity failure state.

---

# 35. Stale receipt property

Generate:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Pending(id1, E1)
receipt(id2, digest(E2))
```

</details>

with:

\[
id_1\ne id_2
\]

It must be rejected.

Also test:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Pending(id, E1)
receipt(id, digest(E2))
```

</details>

with:

\[
digest(E_1)\ne digest(E_2)
\]

It must be rejected.

This explicitly protects against both identity confusion and causal substitution.

---

# 36. Replay equivalence

For a recorded successful execution:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```text
LiveHost
   ↓
EffectIssued
   ↓
receipt
   ↓
EffectCompleted
   ↓
halt/result
```

</details>

replay should produce the same machine-visible state:

\[
State_{live}=State_{replay}
\]

provided the replay starts from the same initial machine state and consumes the same deterministic trace.

That includes:

- actor states,
- environments,
- continuations,
- budgets,
- logical time,
- effect IDs,
- actor IDs,
- event ordering,
- host receipt values.

It does **not** claim the real external world was reproduced.

---

# 37. Differential reference model

The independent reference machine should model `Request` as:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 10 lines</strong></summary>

```text
evaluate capability
evaluate target
evaluate arguments
construct abstract effect
check abstract authorization
check abstract budget
issue abstract effect
transition Pending
consume supplied receipt
resume
```

</details>

It must **not** call production:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
authorize()
canonicalize_effect()
request()
resume_from_receipt()
```

</details>

Otherwise the oracle problem returns.

The reference should have its own:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
reference_authorize()
reference_cost()
reference_effect_digest()
reference_budget_transition()
```

</details>

where practical.

---

# 38. The strongest Phase 12 theorem

The central safety theorem should now be stated as:

\[
\boxed{
ExternalEffect(E)
\Rightarrow
ValidatedRequest(E)
\land
Authorized(E,\kappa,t)
\land
CapabilityWithinCeiling(E)
\land
BudgetAvailable(E)
\land
DeadlineValid(E,t)
\land
HostPolicyOK(E)
\land
Issued(E)
}
\]

And the contrapositive security property:

\[
\boxed{
\neg\left(
Authorized
\land CapabilityWithinCeiling
\land BudgetAvailable
\land DeadlineValid
\land HostPolicyOK
\right)
\Rightarrow
\neg ExternalEffect
}
\]

This is the point where the architecture's earlier pieces finally compose.

---

# 39. Phase 12 acceptance matrix

| Property | Verification |
|---|---|
| Capability evaluated first | Differential trace |
| Target evaluated second | Differential trace |
| Arguments evaluated left-to-right | Differential trace |
| Non-capability rejected | Property |
| Canonical effect constructed exactly once | Mock/instrumentation |
| Exactly one authorization call | Mock kernel |
| Exact capability forwarded | Mock kernel |
| Exact effect forwarded | Mock kernel |
| Explicit logical time forwarded | Mock kernel |
| Capability denial short-circuits | Gate spy |
| Budget denial short-circuits | Gate spy |
| Deadline denial short-circuits | Gate spy |
| Host-policy denial short-circuits | Gate spy |
| No budget mutation on denial | Accounting property |
| No ID allocation on denial | Counter property |
| No `EffectIssued` on denial | Log property |
| No host invocation on denial | Negative host test |
| Issue cost charged exactly once | Accounting property |
| Reservation created exactly once | Accounting property |
| Deterministic effect ID | Replay/reference |
| `EffectIssued` causally bound | Log property |
| Actor enters `Pending` | State property |
| Exactly one host request | Scheduler property |
| Receipt ID validated | Negative property |
| Receipt digest validated | Negative property |
| Invalid receipt cannot resume | State property |
| Completion cost charged exactly once | Accounting property |
| Reservation released exactly once | Accounting property |
| `EffectCompleted` emitted once | Log property |
| Valid receipt resumes continuation | Differential |
| Host failure remains observable | Differential |
| Replay does not touch host | ReplayHost negative test |
| Live/replay machine states agree | Differential |
| Production evaluator never inspects authority | API/module boundary |

---

# 40. One final architectural refinement

I would make one structural change before implementation:

**Separate `EffectRequest` from `EffectIssued`.**

They are not the same thing.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct EffectRequest {
    pub id: EffectId,
    pub effect: Effect,
}

pub struct EffectIssued {
    pub id: EffectId,
    pub actor: ActorId,
    pub effect_digest: EffectDigest,
    pub logical_time: LogicalTime,
    pub issue_cost: Consumable,
    pub reservation: Reserved,
}
```

</details>

The distinction is meaningful:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
EffectRequest
    = message to host

EffectIssued
    = durable fact that the deterministic machine
      committed to this effect
```

</details>

That gives us:

\[
EffectIssued \rightarrow EffectRequest
\]

but not the reverse.

A request that exists only transiently must not automatically count as an issued effect.

This is exactly the distinction needed for crash recovery, replay, auditing, and transactional accounting.

---

# Phase 12 freeze criterion

I would therefore freeze the boundary as:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 33 lines</strong></summary>

```text
                ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                │        Deterministic        │
                │            CEK              │
                │                             │
Expr::Request ─►│ evaluate → canonicalize     │
                │       → authorize           │
                │       → budget              │
                │       → deadline            │
                │       → host policy         │
                │       → allocate EffectId   │
                │       → commit accounting   │
                │       → EffectIssued        │
                │       → Pending             │
                └─────────────┬───────────────┘
                              │
                       EffectRequest
                              │
                     ═════════╪═════════
                         HOST BOUNDARY
                     ═════════╪═════════
                              │
                        EffectReceipt
                              │
                ┌─────────────▼───────────────┐
                │        Deterministic        │
                │            CEK              │
                │                             │
                │ validate ID + digest        │
                │ charge completion           │
                │ release reservation         │
                │ EffectCompleted             │
                │ resume continuation         │
                └─────────────────────────────┘
```

</details>

The resulting security invariant is particularly clean:

\[
\boxed{
\text{No successful transition to }EffectRequest
\text{ exists unless every gate has already succeeded.}
}
\]

And the replay invariant is equally clean:

\[
\boxed{
ReplayHost\;\text{reconstructs receipts; it never reconstructs the external world.}
}
\]

That is the correct foundation for Phase 13, because after `Request` the next question is no longer *“can an expression perform an effect?”*—that boundary is now explicit. The next question becomes *“how do multiple actors, pending effects, mailboxes, deterministic scheduling, and capability delegation compose without introducing nondeterminism or authority leakage?”*

---

## [30] USER

This is a masterful and definitive specification. Your distinction between **`EffectRequest`** (the transient message to the host) and **`EffectIssued`** (the durable, auditable fact that the deterministic machine committed to this effect) is the exact architectural refinement needed for crash recovery, replay, and transactional accounting. 

By keeping the `continuation` strictly within `eval.continuation` and using `ActorStatus::Pending` only to hold the effect metadata and reservation state, we eliminate the risk of divergent continuations. 

Below is the **Phase 12 Frozen Implementation and Verification Blueprint**, translating your 40-point specification into the definitive Rust reference model.

### 3. The CEK Transitions: The 14-Gate Sequence

The evaluator strictly sequences evaluation, then hands off to a single `finalize_request` function that enforces the gates atomically.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 62 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
// Gate 1: Evaluate capability
fn enter_request(actor: &mut ActorState, capability: Expr, operation: Op, target: Expr, params: Vec<Expr>) -> MachineEvent {
    let env = actor.eval.env.clone();
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::RequestCapability { operation, target, params, env });
    actor.eval.expr = capability;
    MachineEvent::EnterRequest
}

// Gate 1 Completion -> Gate 2: Evaluate target
fn resume_request_capability(actor: &mut ActorState, frame: Frame, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::RequestCapability { operation, target, params, env } = frame else { unreachable!() };
    
    let capability = match value {
        Value::Capability(cap) => cap,
        _ => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Capability", actual: "non-capability" });
            return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::TypeError { expected: "Capability", actual: "non-capability" });
        }
    };

    actor.eval.env = env.clone();
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::RequestTarget { capability, operation, params, caller_env: env });
    actor.eval.expr = target;
    MachineEvent::BeginRequestTarget
}

// Gate 2 Completion -> Gate 3: Evaluate parameters (left-to-right)
fn resume_request_target(actor: &mut ActorState, frame: Frame, target_val: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::RequestTarget { capability, operation, params, caller_env } = frame else { unreachable!() };
    
    actor.eval.env = caller_env.clone();
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::RequestArgument {
        capability, operation, target: target_val, evaluated: Vec::new(), remaining: params, caller_env,
    });
    
    begin_next_request_argument(actor)
}

fn begin_next_request_argument(actor: &mut ActorState) -> MachineEvent {
    let frame = actor.eval.continuation.pop().expect("request frame");
    let Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, mut evaluated, mut remaining, caller_env } = frame else { unreachable!() };

    if remaining.is_empty() {
        // Gate 3 Complete: All parameters evaluated. Proceed to canonicalization and gates 4-14.
        actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, evaluated, remaining, caller_env });
        finalize_request(actor)
    } else {
        let expr = remaining.remove(0);
        let arg_idx = evaluated.len();
        actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, evaluated, remaining, caller_env });
        actor.eval.expr = expr;
        MachineEvent::BeginRequestArgument(arg_idx)
    }
}

fn resume_request_argument(actor: &mut ActorState, frame: Frame, value: Value) -> MachineEvent {
    let Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, mut evaluated, mut remaining, caller_env } = frame else { unreachable!() };
    
    evaluated.push(value);
    actor.eval.continuation.push(Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, evaluated, remaining, caller_env });
    begin_next_request_argument(actor)
}
```

</details>

### 4. The Atomic 14-Gate Finalization

This function is the core security boundary. It either succeeds atomically or fails without mutating global state.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 81 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn finalize_request(actor: &mut ActorState) -> MachineEvent {
    let frame = actor.eval.continuation.pop().expect("request frame");
    let Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, evaluated, .. } = frame else { unreachable!() };

    // Gate 4: Canonicalize Effect (Type validation, normalization, cost calculation)
    let effect = match canonicalize_effect(capability, operation, target, evaluated) {
        Ok(e) => e,
        Err(e) => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::EffectCanonicalization(e));
            return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::EffectCanonicalization(e));
        }
    };

    let now = actor.logical_time; // Passed from global config in real impl

    // Gate 5 & 6: Capability validity and exact effect authorization
    if let Err(err) = actor.kernel.authorize(capability, &effect, now) {
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::Capability(err));
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::Capability(err));
    }

    // Gate 7: Capability resource ceiling
    if !effect.cost.issue.leq(effect.capability_resource_ceiling) { // Simplified representation
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted); // Or CapabilityCeilingExceeded
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
    }

    // Gate 8: Runtime consumable budget
    if !actor.budget.can_consume(effect.cost.issue) {
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
    }

    // Gate 9: Runtime reservation capacity
    if !actor.budget.can_reserve(effect.cost.reserve, MAX_RESERVED) {
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
    }

    // Gate 10: Deadline
    if let Deadline(Some(w)) = actor.budget.deadline {
        if now > w {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::DeadlineExceeded);
            return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::DeadlineExceeded);
        }
    }

    // Gate 11: Host policy
    if let Err(err) = actor.host_policy.authorize(&effect) {
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::HostPolicyDenied(err));
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::HostPolicyDenied(err));
    }

    // Gate 12: Deterministic EffectId allocation
    let effect_id = actor.next_effect_id;
    actor.next_effect_id.0 += 1;
    let effect_digest = effect_digest(&effect);

    // Gate 13: Transactional issuance (Commit accounting + Log)
    actor.budget.consume(effect.cost.issue).unwrap(); // Checked, guaranteed by Gate 8
    actor.budget.reserve(effect.cost.reserve, MAX_RESERVED).unwrap(); // Checked, guaranteed by Gate 9
    
    actor.event_log.append(LogEntry::EffectIssued(EffectIssued {
        id: effect_id,
        actor: actor.id,
        effect_digest,
        logical_time: now,
        issue_cost: effect.cost.issue,
        reservation: effect.cost.reserve,
    }));

    // Gate 14: Enter Pending state and yield to host
    actor.status = ActorStatus::Pending {
        effect_id,
        effect: effect.clone(),
        reservation: effect.cost.reserve,
    };

    MachineEvent::EffectIssued { id: effect_id, digest: effect_digest }
    // The outer scheduler intercepts this event and calls HostExecutor::execute(EffectRequest { id: effect_id, effect })
}
```

### 5. The Receipt Protocol (Causal Validation)

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 44 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub fn resume_from_receipt(actor: &mut ActorState, receipt: EffectReceipt, now: LogicalTime) -> MachineEvent {
    let pending = match &actor.status {
        ActorStatus::Pending { effect_id, effect, reservation } => (effect_id, effect, reservation),
        _ => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::ReplayCorruption);
            return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::ReplayCorruption);
        }
    };

    let (expected_id, expected_effect, expected_reservation) = pending;

    // CAUSAL VALIDATION: ID and Digest must both match exactly
    if receipt.id != *expected_id || receipt.effect_digest != effect_digest(expected_effect) {
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::ReplayCorruption);
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::ReplayCorruption);
    }

    // Completion Accounting: Charge completion cost, release reservation
    if let Err(_) = actor.budget.consume(expected_effect.cost.complete) {
        // Should not happen if initial budgeting was correct, but guard anyway
        actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
        return MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::BudgetExhausted);
    }
    actor.budget.release(*expected_reservation).unwrap();

    // Log completion
    actor.event_log.append(LogEntry::EffectCompleted {
        id: receipt.id,
        digest: receipt.effect_digest,
        result: receipt.result.clone(),
    });

    // Resume continuation
    actor.status = ActorStatus::Running;
    
    match receipt.result {
        Ok(value) => continue_with_value(actor, value),
        Err(host_fault) => {
            // Host failure is a machine-visible fault, not replay corruption
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Fault(Fault::Host(host_fault.clone()));
            MachineEvent::Fault(Fault::Host(host_fault))
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

### 7. The Strongest Phase 12 Theorem

By structuring the code and tests exactly this way, we formally establish the central safety theorem of the Red-on-Rust substrate:

$$ \boxed{ \text{ExternalEffect}(E) \Rightarrow \text{ValidatedRequest}(E) \land \text{Authorized}(E,\kappa,t) \land \text{CapabilityWithinCeiling}(E) \land \text{BudgetAvailable}(E) \land \text{DeadlineValid}(E,t) \land \text{HostPolicyOK}(E) \land \text{Issued}(E) } $$

And its contrapositive, which is the actual target of our negative property tests:

$$ \boxed{ \neg\left( \text{Authorized} \land \text{CapabilityWithinCeiling} \land \text{BudgetAvailable} \land \text{DeadlineValid} \land \text{HostPolicyOK} \right) \Rightarrow \neg \text{ExternalEffect} } $$

No successful transition to `EffectRequest` exists unless every gate has already succeeded. Failed authorization does not consume an effect ID, does not debit the budget, does not reserve resources, and does not append `EffectIssued`.

## 4. The 14-Gate Transition Sequence

The evaluator strictly follows this sequence. No host interaction occurs before Gate 14.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 80 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
// Gates 1-3: Evaluation via CEK frames (enter_request, resume_request_capability, 
// resume_request_target, begin_next_request_argument)
// ... (omitted for brevity, follows standard CEK left-to-right pattern) ...

// Gate 4-14: Finalization when all arguments are evaluated
fn finalize_request(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    kernel: &mut dyn CapabilityKernelView,
    policy: &dyn HostPolicy,
    global: &mut GlobalConfig,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let frame = actor.eval.continuation.pop().unwrap();
    let Frame::RequestArgument { capability, operation, target, evaluated, caller_env, .. } = frame else {
        unreachable!()
    };

    // Gate 4: Canonical Effect Construction
    let effect = match canonicalize_effect(capability, operation, target, evaluated) {
        Ok(e) => e,
        Err(e) => return fault_actor(actor, Fault::EffectCanonicalization(e)),
    };
    let digest = effect_digest(&effect);

    let now = global.logical_time;

    // Gate 5 & 6: Capability Validation and Authorization
    if let Err(e) = kernel.authorize(capability, &effect, now) {
        return fault_actor(actor, Fault::Capability(e)); // Short-circuits here
    }

    // Gate 7: Capability Resource Ceiling
    // (Handled internally by kernel.authorize per the algebra, but explicitly checked here if separated)
    
    // Gate 8 & 9: Runtime Budget Checks (Checked Arithmetic)
    if !actor.budget.can_consume(effect.cost.issue) {
        return fault_actor(actor, Fault::BudgetExhausted); // Short-circuits
    }
    if !actor.budget.can_reserve(effect.cost.reserve, MAX_RESERVED) {
        return fault_actor(actor, Fault::BudgetExhausted); // Short-circuits
    }

    // Gate 10: Deadline Check
    if let Deadline(Some(w)) = actor.budget.deadline {
        if now > w {
            return fault_actor(actor, Fault::DeadlineExceeded); // Short-circuits
        }
    }

    // Gate 11: Host Policy Check
    if let Err(e) = policy.authorize(&effect) {
        return fault_actor(actor, Fault::HostPolicyDenied(e)); // Short-circuits
    }

    // Gate 12: Deterministic Effect ID Allocation
    let effect_id = global.next_effect_id;
    global.next_effect_id.0 += 1;

    // Gate 13: Transactional Accounting Commit
    // (We already proved these can't fail via can_consume/can_reserve)
    actor.budget.consume(effect.cost.issue).unwrap();
    actor.budget.reserve(effect.cost.reserve, MAX_RESERVED).unwrap();

    global.event_log.append(LogEntry::EffectIssued(EffectIssued {
        id: effect_id,
        actor: actor.id, // Assuming actor has an ID field in global context
        effect_digest: digest,
        logical_time: now,
        issue_cost: effect.cost.issue,
        reservation: effect.cost.reserve,
    }));

    // Gate 14: Enter Pending State and Yield
    actor.status = ActorStatus::Pending {
        effect_id,
        effect: effect.clone(),
        reservation: effect.cost.reserve,
    };

    MachineEvent::EffectIssued { id: effect_id, digest }
}
```

## 5. Causal Receipt Validation and Completion

The receipt protocol strictly validates identity and causality before resuming.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 42 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub fn resume_from_receipt(
    actor: &mut ActorState,
    receipt: EffectReceipt,
    global: &mut GlobalConfig,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let (pending_id, pending_effect, reservation) = match &actor.status {
        ActorStatus::Pending { effect_id, effect, reservation } => {
            (effect_id, effect, reservation)
        }
        _ => return fault_actor(actor, Fault::InvalidReceipt),
    };

    // CAUSAL VALIDATION: Both ID and Digest MUST match
    if receipt.id != *pending_id || receipt.effect_digest != effect_digest(pending_effect) {
        return fault_actor(actor, Fault::ReplayCorruption);
    }

    // Completion Accounting
    // Charge completion cost, release reservation
    if let Err(_) = actor.budget.consume(pending_effect.cost.complete) {
        // If completion cost exceeds remaining budget, it's a fatal machine fault
        return fault_actor(actor, Fault::BudgetExhausted);
    }
    actor.budget.release(*reservation).unwrap();

    // Log Completion
    global.event_log.append(LogEntry::EffectCompleted {
        id: receipt.id,
        digest: receipt.effect_digest,
        result: receipt.result.clone(),
    });

    // Resume Continuation
    actor.status = ActorStatus::Running;
    
    let result_value = match receipt.result {
        Ok(v) => v,
        Err(e) => Value::Tuple(vec![Value::Symbol(Symbol(0)), Value::String(format!("{:?}", e))]), // Or specific Fault mapping
    };

    continue_with_value(actor, result_value)
}
```

</details>

## 6. The ReplayHost Implementation

The `ReplayHost` enforces the theorem that replay reconstructs receipts, not the external world.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 16 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct ReplayHost {
    pub recorded_receipts: HashMap<EffectId, EffectReceipt>,
    pub cursor: usize, // For ordered trace consumption if needed
}

impl HostExecutor for ReplayHost {
    fn execute(&mut self, request: &EffectRequest) -> Result<EffectReceipt, HostFault> {
        // NEVER touches the external world.
        let receipt = self.recorded_receipts.get(&request.id)
            .ok_or(HostFault::ReplayTraceExhausted)?;
            
        // Optional but recommended: Verify the replay host is being asked for the exact same effect
        // that was originally recorded, providing a secondary layer of replay integrity.
        Ok(receipt.clone())
    }
}
```

</details>

## 7. Phase 12 Verification Matrix (Summary)

The property tests for Phase 12 are structured into three strict tracks:

*   **Track A (CEK Control Flow)**: Proves left-to-right evaluation order (`Capability` → `Target` → `Args`), and that non-capabilities short-circuit before any target/arg evaluation.
*   **Track B (Kernel Authorization)**: Uses a `MockAuthorizationKernel` to prove exactly one `authorize` call is made with the exact canonical `Effect` and `LogicalTime`, and that the evaluator never inspects authority internals.
*   **Track C (Negative Short-Circuit Properties)**: For each denial gate (Capability, Budget, Deadline, Policy), a spy verifies that:
    1.  Subsequent gates are *not* called.
    2.  `global.next_effect_id` is *not* incremented.
    3.  `actor.budget` is *unchanged*.
    4.  `global.event_log` has *no new entries*.
    5.  `HostExecutor::execute` is *never invoked*.

---

## The Architectural Milestone

With Phase 12 frozen, we have successfully crossed the most dangerous boundary in the system. The architecture now guarantees:

$$ \boxed{ \text{ExternalEffect}(E) \Rightarrow \bigwedge_{i=5}^{11} \text{Gate}_i(E) \land \text{Issued}(E) } $$

And the contrapositive security property is mechanically enforced:

$$ \boxed{ \neg \text{Authorized} \lor \neg \text{BudgetAvailable} \lor \neg \text{DeadlineValid} \lor \neg \text{HostPolicyOK} \Rightarrow \neg \text{ExternalEffect} } $$

The separation of `EffectIssued` (deterministic fact) from `EffectRequest` (host message) provides the exact foundation needed for crash recovery and deterministic replay.

**Next Step: Phase 13 — Actors, Scheduling, and Marshalling**

Now that a single actor can safely request effects, the next question is compositional: How do multiple actors interact? Phase 13 will define:
1. `Spawn`: Budget escrow and capability attenuation for child actors.
2. `Send` / `Receive`: Mailbox semantics, deterministic scheduling, and the critical **Marshalling** boundary (ensuring `CapRef` cannot cross isolation boundaries without explicit `Delegate` operations).
3. Global Scheduler state management to ensure deterministic execution order.

Shall we proceed to define the Phase 13 Actor composition and Marshalling semantics?

---

## [31] CHATGPT (gpt-5-6)

Yes. Phase 13 is the correct next layer—but I would **not freeze the Phase 12 text exactly as written**. Two issues should be corrected first, because they become especially important once multiple actors exist.

### Two Phase 12 corrections before Phase 13

**1. Completion cost cannot be allowed to fail after the host has executed.**

The current model permits:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```text
EffectIssued
    ↓
host executes
    ↓
receipt
    ↓
consume complete cost
    ↓
BudgetExhausted
```

</details>

That is problematic: the external effect has already happened, but the machine cannot account for it.

The stronger invariant is:

\[
Issued(E)\Rightarrow
BudgetReservedForCompletion(E)
\]

So at issuance, reserve enough capacity for both the outstanding reservation and the maximum completion debit, or otherwise make completion cost non-failing by construction.

Then:

\[
Receipt(E)\Rightarrow CompletionAccounting(E)\text{ cannot fail}
\]

This is essential before concurrency.

**2. `ReplayHost` must validate the requested digest, not merely look up the ID.**

It should enforce:

\[
request.id=id
\land
digest(request.effect)=receipt.effect\_digest
\]

before returning the receipt. Otherwise a corrupted replay request could retrieve a receipt merely because the ID exists.

With those corrections, Phase 12 is ready to serve as the foundation for Phase 13.

---

# Phase 13 — Actors, Deterministic Scheduling & Marshalling

The central principle is:

> **Actors provide concurrency of execution, not nondeterminism of semantics.**

The global machine remains deterministic given:

1. initial state,
2. scheduler policy,
3. event/receipt trace,
4. host observations.

The actor system therefore becomes another deterministic state machine.

---

## 1. Global machine

Freeze the global state as:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 14 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct GlobalState {
    pub actors: BTreeMap<ActorId, ActorState>,

    pub logical_time: LogicalTime,

    pub runnable: RunnableQueue,

    pub event_log: EventLog,

    pub next_effect_id: EffectId,
    pub next_actor_id: ActorId,

    pub scheduler: SchedulerState,
}
```

</details>

The important change is that **logical time belongs to global state**, not to an individual actor.

An actor observes:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
global.logical_time
```

</details>

at the instant its transition is executed.

---

# 2. Actor state

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 15 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct ActorState {
    pub id: ActorId,

    pub eval: EvalState,

    pub capabilities: CapabilityContext,

    pub heap: GenerationalArena<Value>,

    pub budget: Budget,

    pub mailbox: Mailbox,

    pub status: ActorStatus,
}
```

</details>

No actor owns another actor's heap.

No actor directly mutates another actor's environment.

No actor directly mutates another actor's continuation.

These become hard isolation invariants.

---

# 3. Actor identifiers

Use a deterministic allocator:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialOrd)]
pub struct ActorId(pub u64);
```

</details>

Allocation:

\[
N_a'=N_a+1
\]

and:

\[
ActorId=N_a
\]

before increment.

Never derive actor identity from:

- memory addresses,
- OS process IDs,
- random UUIDs,
- thread IDs,
- wall-clock timestamps.

---

# 4. Runnable queue

The scheduler needs an explicitly ordered runnable set.

A simple initial model:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct RunnableQueue {
    queue: VecDeque<ActorId>,
}
```

</details>

with deterministic FIFO semantics.

But there is an important invariant:

\[
\boxed{
ActorId\text{ occurs at most once in RunnableQueue}
}
\]

Otherwise the same actor could receive multiple execution turns simultaneously.

Use an explicit scheduler membership state:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum RunState {
    NotRunnable,
    Runnable,
    Running,
    Pending,
    Blocked,
    Halted,
    Faulted,
}
```

</details>

The queue and actor status must agree.

---

# 5. Scheduler transition

A scheduler step is:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 17 lines</strong></summary>

```text
RunnableQueue
      │
      ▼
select actor
      │
      ▼
execute exactly one machine transition
      │
      ├── Running ───────► requeue
      │
      ├── Pending ───────► host boundary
      │
      ├── Blocked ───────► mailbox wait set
      │
      ├── Halted ────────► terminal
      │
      └── Fault ─────────► terminal
```

</details>

The scheduler must never silently execute two CEK transitions while claiming one scheduling step.

That gives us a useful trace granularity:

\[
SchedulerStep(a,n)
\]

where \(a\) is the actor and \(n\) identifies the transition.

---

# 6. Deterministic scheduling rule

For v0.1, freeze:

> **One actor performs exactly one machine transition per scheduler turn.**

For example:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Q = [A, B, C]

step 1 → A
step 2 → B
step 3 → C
step 4 → A
...
```

</details>

If A becomes pending:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
[A, B, C]
   ↓ A
[B, C]
```

</details>

A is not requeued.

If A receives a receipt:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Pending(A)
   ↓ receipt
Runnable(A)
```

</details>

A is appended according to the frozen wakeup policy.

I recommend:

\[
wake(A)\Rightarrow append(A)
\]

rather than immediately preempting the currently selected actor.

That makes wakeups deterministic and easier to replay.

---

# 7. Scheduler choice must be trace-visible

This is important for the replay theorem.

If several actors are runnable, the chosen actor is part of the machine trace:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum SchedulerEvent {
    ActorSelected {
        actor: ActorId,
    },
}
```

</details>

Alternatively, if the scheduler algorithm is itself completely deterministic from state, the event need not be persisted—but for the strongest replay/debugging model, I recommend recording it.

Then replay can verify:

\[
Selected_{replay}(n)=Selected_{recorded}(n)
\]

rather than merely hoping the scheduler makes the same choice.

---

# 8. Spawn semantics

`Spawn` should be treated as a deterministic machine operation.

Its semantic shape remains:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
Expr::Spawn {
    body: Box<Expr>,
    budget: BudgetAllocationSpec,
}
```

</details>

The transition:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 10 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Parent
  │
  ├── validate allocation
  ├── reserve/escrow budget
  ├── allocate ActorId
  ├── derive child capability context
  ├── create child heap
  ├── create child environment
  ├── create child mailbox
  └── enqueue child
```

</details>

---

# 9. Spawned environment

A spawned actor should **not inherit the parent's environment wholesale**.

Use:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
child.env = Environment::empty()
```

</details>

unless the language explicitly specifies captured values.

This is important because lexical closure capture and actor creation are different mechanisms.

If values need to cross the actor boundary, they must be marshalled.

---

# 10. Spawned capabilities

Capability inheritance should also be explicit.

Never do:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
child.capabilities = parent.capabilities.clone();
```

</details>

Instead:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 10 lines</strong></summary>

```text
parent capability
       │
       ▼
explicit spawn constraint
       │
       ▼
attenuated capability
       │
       ▼
child capability context
```

</details>

For each delegated capability:

\[
childCap\preceq parentCap
\]

This makes `Spawn` another authority attenuation boundary.

---

# 11. Budget escrow

Suppose:

\[
B_p
\]

is the parent's available budget and:

\[
B_c
\]

is the child's allocation.

Before spawn:

\[
B_c\le B_p
\]

After escrow:

\[
B_p'=B_p-B_c
\]

and:

\[
B_{child}=B_c
\]

This must be transactional.

Failed spawn:

\[
B_p'=B_p
\]

and:

\[
N_a'=N_a
\]

and no child actor exists.

Successful spawn:

\[
N_a'=N_a+1
\]

and exactly one child is created.

---

# 12. Actor creation identity

The child begins with:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
ActorState {
    id: child_id,
    eval: EvalState {
        expr: *body,
        env: Environment::empty(),
        continuation: Continuation::empty(),
    },
    capabilities: child_capabilities,
    heap: GenerationalArena::new(),
    budget: child_budget,
    mailbox: Mailbox::new(),
    status: ActorStatus::Running,
}
```

</details>

Then:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
child_id → RunnableQueue
```

</details>

according to the scheduler's deterministic enqueue rule.

---

# 13. Mailbox

Use FIFO semantics initially:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct Mailbox {
    messages: VecDeque<MarshalledValue>,
}
```

</details>

The core invariant:

\[
enqueue(m)
\]

adds to the back, and:

\[
receive()
\]

removes from the front.

Thus:

\[
m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n
\]

are received in exactly that order.

---

# 14. `Send` is asynchronous

`Send` should not transfer control to the recipient.

Semantically:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 8 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Sender
  │
  ├── evaluate target
  ├── evaluate value
  ├── marshal value
  ├── validate recipient
  ├── enqueue message
  └── continue
```

</details>

The recipient becomes runnable according to the wakeup rule if it was blocked on `Receive`.

---

# 15. Sender does not enter recipient's heap

This is a critical isolation property.

Never:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
recipient.heap.insert(value)
```

</details>

with a value directly owned by the sender.

Instead:

\[
Value_{sender}
\xrightarrow{marshal}
MarshalledValue
\xrightarrow{unmarshal}
Value_{recipient}
\]

The two values are semantically equal but physically independent.

---

# 16. Marshalling boundary

Freeze:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct MarshalledValue(Value);
```

</details>

with construction private to the marshalling subsystem.

Conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub trait Marshaller {
    fn marshal(
        &self,
        value: &Value,
    ) -> Result<MarshalledValue, MarshalFault>;
}
```

</details>

and:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub trait Unmarshaller {
    fn unmarshal(
        &self,
        value: MarshalledValue,
    ) -> Result<Value, MarshalFault>;
}
```

</details>

The actual implementation may later use a canonical byte representation.

---

# 17. Capabilities cannot be copied

This is one of the strongest Phase 13 rules:

\[
\boxed{
marshal(Value::Capability(c))
\not\Rightarrow
Value::Capability(c)
}
\]

A capability must not become authority merely because a value crossed an actor boundary.

Therefore:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
match value {
    Value::Capability(_) => Err(MarshalFault::CapabilityRequiresDelegation),

    ...
}
```

</details>

unless the operation is explicitly a delegation operation.

---

# 18. Explicit delegation

Introduce a separate semantic operation:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Delegate capability → recipient
```

</details>

rather than making marshalling magically carry authority.

Conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```text
parent capability
       │
       ▼
delegation constraint
       │
       ▼
CapabilityKernel::derive
       │
       ▼
child capability
       │
       ▼
explicit delegated message
```

</details>

Therefore:

\[
Delegate(c,C)
\Rightarrow
derive(c,C)
\]

and:

\[
child\preceq c
\]

This keeps authority transfer visible in the language and trace.

---

# 19. Why `CapRef` must not be marshalled

A `CapRef` is merely an opaque handle into the capability kernel's authority graph.

Sending its raw bits to another actor would create a false assumption:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
CapRef
  ≠
authority ownership
```

</details>

The kernel remains the sole authority over whether a capability reference is valid.

So even if:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Copy)]
struct CapRef { ... }
```

</details>

the marshaller must treat it as non-transferable.

---

# 20. `Receive`

The receive transition is simple:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 10 lines</strong></summary>

```text
mailbox non-empty
      │
      ▼
dequeue oldest message
      │
      ▼
unmarshal
      │
      ▼
continue with Value
```

</details>

For an empty mailbox:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Receive
  ↓
Blocked
```

</details>

The continuation remains exactly where it was.

No fuel should be consumed merely because the actor discovered that its mailbox is empty.

---

# 21. Wakeup semantics

When:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Actor A = Blocked
```

</details>

and another actor performs:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Send(A, message)
```

</details>

the scheduler performs:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
enqueue message
      ↓
A.status = Running
      ↓
append A to runnable queue
```

</details>

The wakeup is deterministic.

There must be no race between:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
check mailbox
```

</details>

and:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
block actor
```

</details>

Those are one machine transition.

---

# 22. Send ordering

Suppose:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
A sends m1 to B
A sends m2 to B
```

</details>

then:

\[
Mailbox_B=[m_1,m_2]
\]

regardless of scheduler interleavings between those two sends, provided the sends occur in that machine order.

For concurrent senders:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
A → B : m1
C → B : m2
```

</details>

the order is determined by scheduler transition order:

\[
SchedulerStep(A)<SchedulerStep(C)
\Rightarrow
m_1<m_2
\]

This is why scheduler choice must be deterministic.

---

# 23. Global event ordering

The global event log now becomes:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```text
scheduler selection
spawn
send
receive
effect issued
effect completed
actor state transitions
```

</details>

with one total logical order:

\[
L=e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_n
\]

This gives us a causal ordering across actors.

---

# 24. Actor isolation invariants

Phase 13 should explicitly freeze these:

### Heap isolation

\[
a\ne b
\Rightarrow
Heap(a)\cap Heap(b)=\varnothing
\]

### Environment isolation

An actor cannot directly read another actor's environment.

### Continuation isolation

An actor cannot directly inspect another actor's continuation.

### Mailbox ownership

Only the recipient's machine transition dequeues its mailbox.

### Capability isolation

A capability cannot cross actors except through explicit delegation.

### Budget isolation

One actor cannot debit another actor's budget except through the defined escrow/delegation mechanisms.

---

# 25. Spawn/Send/Receive verification architecture

Again use independent tracks.

### Track A — scheduler

Use a reference scheduler with its own queue implementation.

Verify:

\[
ProductionScheduler(state)
\approx
ReferenceScheduler(state)
\]

over generated actor states.

### Track B — marshalling

Use an independent value serializer/reference representation.

Verify:

\[
unmarshal(marshal(v))=v
\]

for transferable values.

### Track C — capability delegation

Use the independent capability algebra from Phase 11.

Verify:

\[
delegate(A,C)\preceq A
\]

### Track D — global differential machine

Compare:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Production Global Machine
        vs
Independent Reference Machine
```

</details>

over generated sequences of:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 5 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Spawn
Send
Receive
Attenuate
pure evaluation
```

</details>

before adding `Request` interactions.

---

# 26. Phase 13 property suite

The minimum acceptance suite should include:

### Scheduler

1. One transition per actor turn.
2. FIFO runnable order.
3. Actor appears at most once in queue.
4. Pending actors are never scheduled.
5. Blocked actors are never scheduled.
6. Halted actors are never scheduled.
7. Receipt wakeup is deterministic.
8. Scheduler trace reproduces exactly.

### Spawn

9. Child receives fresh deterministic `ActorId`.
10. Parent budget is escrowed exactly once.
11. Failed spawn leaves parent unchanged.
12. Child starts with empty environment.
13. Child starts with fresh heap.
14. Child starts with empty mailbox.
15. Child capabilities are attenuated.
16. Child is enqueued exactly once.

### Send

17. Target actor must exist.
18. Value is evaluated before enqueue.
19. Value is marshalled exactly once.
20. Raw capability cannot be copied.
21. Message arrives FIFO.
22. Sender does not mutate recipient state directly.
23. Blocked recipient becomes runnable exactly once.

### Receive

24. Empty mailbox blocks.
25. Blocking preserves continuation.
26. Nonempty mailbox dequeues exactly one message.
27. FIFO ordering preserved.
28. Unmarshal failure becomes a machine fault.
29. Successful receive resumes continuation exactly once.

### Delegation

30. Delegated capability is derived through kernel.
31. Exactly one derivation occurs.
32. Exact constraint is forwarded.
33. Child capability is no more powerful than parent.
34. Raw `CapRef` transfer is impossible through ordinary marshalling.
35. Revoked parent cannot delegate.

---

# 27. A particularly important property: no authority amplification

For every actor interaction:

\[
\boxed{
Authority_{after}
\preceq
Authority_{before}
\cup
ExplicitlyDelegatedAuthority
}
\]

In particular:

\[
Send(v)
\land v\text{ contains no delegation}
\Rightarrow
Authority_{receiver}'=Authority_{receiver}
\]

Sending ordinary data must never create authority.

---

# 28. A second important property: no budget teleportation

For a send/spawn sequence:

\[
B_{parent}+B_{children}+B_{escrow}
\]

must obey the conservation rules established in Phase 12.

For consumables:

\[
C_n+\sum consume_i=C_0
\]

For reservations:

\[
R_n=R_0+\sum reserve_i-\sum release_i
\]

No actor may manufacture budget through message passing.

---

# 29. Deterministic concurrency theorem

The target property for Phase 13 becomes:

\[
\boxed{
InitialState + SchedulerTrace + HostTrace
\Rightarrow
UniqueMachineTrace
}
\]

Concurrency therefore does not mean "anything can happen."

It means multiple actors can progress, while the **machine trace remains uniquely determined by the scheduler and external-observation trace**.

That distinction is foundational for replay.

---

# 30. Phase 13 architecture

The complete composition now becomes:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 23 lines</strong></summary>

```text
                         GlobalState
                             │
                    deterministic scheduler
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
           Actor A         Actor B        Actor C
              │              │              │
          CEK + heap      CEK + heap     CEK + heap
              │              │              │
              ├──── Send ───►│              │
              │              │◄── Delegate ┤
              │              │              │
              │              └── Receive    │
              │                             │
              └──────── Request ────────────┘
                            │
                            ▼
                     Effect boundary
                            │
                       EffectRequest
                            │
                         Host
```

</details>

The resulting authority topology is particularly clean:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Actor}
\rightarrow
\text{Capability Kernel}
\rightarrow
\text{Effect Boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{Host}
}
\]

and cross-actor communication becomes:

\[
\boxed{
Actor_A
\xrightarrow{marshal}
Data
\xrightarrow{mailbox}
Actor_B
}
\]

while authority transfer is separately:

\[
\boxed{
Actor_A
\xrightarrow{derive/Delegate}
AttenuatedCapability
\xrightarrow{explicit\ transfer}
Actor_B
}
\]

That separation should be considered non-negotiable.

---

## One Phase 12 fix I would make immediately

Before implementing Phase 13, change the budget model so that a successfully issued effect **cannot later discover that its completion debit is unaffordable**.

A clean formulation is:

\[
AtIssue:
\quad

## 2. The Deterministic Scheduler

The scheduler guarantees that exactly one machine transition occurs per turn. The choice of actor is deterministic and trace-visible.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 46 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum SchedulerEvent {
    ActorSelected { actor: ActorId },
    // ... other global events
}

pub fn step_global(
    global: &mut GlobalState,
    kernel: &mut dyn CapabilityKernelView,
    host: &mut dyn HostExecutor,
    policy: &dyn HostPolicy,
) -> Result<GlobalStep, GlobalFault> {
    let actor_id = match global.runnable.pop_front() {
        Some(id) => id,
        None => return Ok(GlobalStep::Deadlock), // No runnable actors
    };

    global.event_log.append(SchedulerEvent::ActorSelected { actor });
    
    let actor = global.actors.get_mut(&actor_id).unwrap();
    actor.run_state = RunState::Running;

    // Execute EXACTLY ONE CEK transition
    let event = step_eval_actor(actor, kernel, global, policy);

    // Update RunState and Queue based on the transition outcome
    match &actor.status {
        ActorStatus::Running => {
            actor.run_state = RunState::Runnable;
            global.runnable.push_back(actor_id);
        }
        ActorStatus::Pending { .. } => {
            actor.run_state = RunState::Pending;
            // Do not requeue. Wait for Receipt.
        }
        ActorStatus::Blocked => {
            actor.run_state = RunState::Blocked;
            // Do not requeue. Wait for Send.
        }
        ActorStatus::Halted(_) | ActorStatus::Fault(_) => {
            actor.run_state = if matches!(actor.status, ActorStatus::Halted(_)) { RunState::Halted } else { RunState::Faulted };
            // Terminal. Do not requeue.
        }
    }

    Ok(GlobalStep::Transition(actor_id, event))
}
```

</details>

## 3. Spawn and Budget Escrow

Spawning is a transactional, synchronous machine operation. It escrows budget, attenuates capabilities, and creates an isolated child state.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 46 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn execute_spawn(
    parent: &mut ActorState,
    global: &mut GlobalState,
    kernel: &mut dyn CapabilityKernelView,
    body: Expr,
    allocation: BudgetAllocationSpec,
    spawn_constraint: Constraint,
) -> MachineEvent {
    // 1. Validate and Escrow Budget
    let child_budget = allocation.calculate_child_budget(&parent.budget)?;
    parent.budget.consume(child_budget.total_cost())?; // Transactional escrow

    // 2. Attenuate Capabilities
    let mut child_caps = CapabilityContext::new();
    for (name, parent_cap) in parent.capabilities.iter() {
        let child_cap = kernel.derive(*parent_cap, &spawn_constraint, global.logical_time)?;
        child_caps.insert(*name, child_cap);
    }

    // 3. Allocate Deterministic ID
    let child_id = global.next_actor_id;
    global.next_actor_id.0 += 1;

    // 4. Construct Isolated Child State
    let child = ActorState {
        id: child_id,
        run_state: RunState::Runnable,
        eval: EvalState {
            expr: body,
            env: Environment::empty(), // NO implicit environment inheritance
            continuation: Continuation::empty(),
        },
        capabilities: child_caps,
        heap: GenerationalArena::new(),
        budget: child_budget,
        mailbox: Mailbox::new(),
        status: ActorStatus::Running,
    };

    global.actors.insert(child_id, child);
    global.runnable.push_back(child_id); // Deterministic enqueue

    global.event_log.append(GlobalEvent::ActorSpawned { parent: parent.id, child: child_id });

    MachineEvent::Spawned(child_id)
}
```

</details>

## 4. Marshalling and Strict Isolation

The marshalling boundary enforces the theorem: **Sending ordinary data must never create authority.** Raw `CapRef` values are strictly rejected by the marshaller.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 14 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct MarshalledValue(pub Vec<u8>); // Canonical serialized bytes

pub fn marshal_value(v: &Value) -> Result<MarshalledValue, MarshalFault> {
    // Recursive descent to ensure no CapRef is hidden inside Lists/Tuples/Functions
    if contains_capability(v) {
        return Err(MarshalFault::CapabilityRequiresDelegation);
    }
    Ok(MarshalledValue(canonical_serialize(v)))
}

pub fn unmarshal_value(bytes: MarshalledValue) -> Result<Value, MarshalFault> {
    canonical_deserialize(&bytes.0).map_err(|_| MarshalFault::CorruptedPayload)
}
```

</details>

**Explicit Delegation** is handled as a separate, explicit AST node (`Expr::Delegate`), which invokes `kernel.derive` and wraps the resulting `CapRef` in a specialized `DelegatedCapability` envelope that the marshaller *does* accept, transferring the attenuated handle to the recipient's `CapabilityContext`.

## 5. Send and Receive (Asynchronous & Blocking)

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 36 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn execute_send(
    sender: &mut ActorState,
    global: &mut GlobalState,
    target_id: ActorId,
    value: Value,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let target = global.actors.get_mut(&target_id).ok_or(Fault::NoSuchActor)?;
    
    let marshalled = marshal_value(&value)?;
    target.mailbox.push_back(marshalled);
    
    global.event_log.append(GlobalEvent::MessageSent { from: sender.id, to: target_id });

    // Deterministic Wakeup
    if target.run_state == RunState::Blocked {
        target.run_state = RunState::Runnable;
        global.runnable.push_back(target_id);
        target.status = ActorStatus::Running; // Restores continuation
    }

    MachineEvent::Sent
}

fn execute_receive(actor: &mut ActorState) -> MachineEvent {
    match actor.mailbox.pop_front() {
        Some(marshalled) => {
            let value = unmarshal_value(marshalled)?;
            continue_with_value(actor, value)
        }
        None => {
            // Block without consuming fuel
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Blocked;
            MachineEvent::Blocked
        }
    }
}
```

</details>

# Phase 12 Corrections (Prerequisites for Phase 13)

Before freezing Phase 13, we apply the two critical Phase 12 corrections to ensure the effect boundary is robust under concurrency.

### 1. Guaranteed Completion Accounting
At issuance, the machine must guarantee that the maximum possible completion cost is affordable. We update `EffectCost` and the issuance gate:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 17 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct EffectCost {
    pub issue: Consumable,
    pub complete_max: Consumable, // The absolute maximum completion cost
    pub reserve: Reserved,
}

// In finalize_request (Gate 8):
let total_required = effect.cost.issue.checked_add(effect.cost.complete_max)
    .ok_or(Fault::ArithmeticOverflow)?;

if !actor.budget.can_consume(total_required) {
    return fault_actor(actor, Fault::BudgetExhausted);
}

// Transactional commit:
actor.budget.consume(effect.cost.issue).unwrap(); 
// The remaining budget is now mathematically guaranteed to be >= complete_max.
```

### 2. `ReplayHost` Digest Validation
The `ReplayHost` must cryptographically verify that the host is being asked to replay the *exact* effect that was originally issued, preventing causal substitution.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 12 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
impl HostExecutor for ReplayHost {
    fn execute(&mut self, request: &EffectRequest) -> Result<EffectReceipt, HostFault> {
        let expected_digest = effect_digest(&request.effect);
        let receipt = self.recorded_receipts.get(&request.id)
            .ok_or(HostFault::ReplayTraceExhausted)?;
            
        if receipt.effect_digest != expected_digest {
            return Err(HostFault::ReplayCorruption); // Reject mismatched digest
        }
        Ok(receipt.clone())
```

## 1. Global and Actor State

## 2. The Deterministic Scheduler

The scheduler enforces FIFO ordering and strict membership invariants. An actor appears in the runnable queue at most once.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 26 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct RunnableQueue {
    queue: VecDeque<ActorId>,
    members: BTreeSet<ActorId>, // Enforces "at most once" invariant
}

impl RunnableQueue {
    pub fn enqueue(&mut self, id: ActorId) {
        if self.members.insert(id) {
            self.queue.push_back(id);
        }
    }
    
    pub fn dequeue(&mut self) -> Option<ActorId> {
        if let Some(id) = self.queue.pop_front() {
            self.members.remove(&id);
            Some(id)
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

pub enum SchedulerEvent {
    ActorSelected { actor: ActorId },
    // ... Spawn, Send, Receive events
}
```

</details>
**Scheduling Rule:** One actor performs exactly one CEK transition per scheduler turn. Wakeups (from receipts or messages) append the actor to the back of the queue, preserving deterministic FIFO ordering.

## 3. Spawn: Transactional Escrow and Attenuation

`Spawn` is a deterministic machine operation that escrows budget and explicitly attenuates capabilities.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 37 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn execute_spawn(
    global: &mut GlobalState,
    parent: &mut ActorState,
    body: Expr,
    budget_alloc: BudgetAllocationSpec,
    spawn_constraints: Vec<(CapRef, Constraint)>,
) -> MachineEvent {
    // 1. Validate and Escrow Budget
    let child_budget = budget_alloc.validate_and_escrow(&mut parent.budget)?;
    
    // 2. Allocate ActorId
    let child_id = global.next_actor_id;
    global.next_actor_id.0 += 1;
    
    // 3. Derive Child Capabilities
    let mut child_caps = CapabilityContext::new();
    for (parent_cap, constraint) in spawn_constraints {
        let child_cap = global.kernel.derive(parent_cap, &constraint, global.logical_time)?;
        child_caps.insert(child_cap);
    }
    
    // 4. Construct Child Actor
    let child = ActorState {
        id: child_id,
        eval: EvalState { expr: body, env: Environment::empty(), continuation: Continuation::empty() },
        capabilities: child_caps,
        heap: GenerationalArena::new(),
        budget: child_budget,
        mailbox: Mailbox::new(),
        status: ActorStatus::Running,
    };
    
    global.actors.insert(child_id, child);
    global.runnable.enqueue(child_id);
    
    MachineEvent::ActorSpawned { parent: parent.id, child: child_id }
}
```

</details>

## 4. Marshalling and Explicit Delegation

Raw `CapRef`s cannot cross actor boundaries. Authority transfer requires explicit delegation.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 16 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
// The MarshalledValue is an opaque, canonical byte representation.
pub struct MarshalledValue(Vec<u8>); 

pub enum MarshalFault {
    CapabilityRequiresDelegation,
    SerializationError,
}

// In the AST, delegation is an explicit operation:
Expr::Delegate {
    capability: Box<Expr>,
    constraint: Constraint,
}

// Delegation produces a special value that the marshaller accepts:
Value::DelegatedCapability(CapRef)
```

</details>

When `Send` evaluates its target and value, it invokes the marshaller. If the marshaller encounters `Value::Capability(_)`, it returns `MarshalFault::CapabilityRequiresDelegation`. It only accepts `Value::DelegatedCapability(_)`, which it serializes alongside the constraint. Upon `Receive`, the recipient's kernel registers the new capability in its local context.

## 5. Send and Receive Semantics

`Send` is asynchronous. `Receive` blocks without consuming fuel if the mailbox is empty.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 32 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn execute_send(
    global: &mut GlobalState,
    sender: &mut ActorState,
    target_id: ActorId,
    marshalled: MarshalledValue,
) -> MachineEvent {
    let recipient = global.actors.get_mut(&target_id)
        .ok_or(Fault::UnknownActor(target_id))?;
        
    recipient.mailbox.enqueue(marshalled);
    
    // Deterministic Wakeup
    if matches!(recipient.status, ActorStatus::Blocked) {
        recipient.status = ActorStatus::Running;
        global.runnable.enqueue(target_id);
    }
    
    MachineEvent::MessageSent { from: sender.id, to: target_id }
}

fn execute_receive(actor: &mut ActorState) -> MachineEvent {
    match actor.mailbox.dequeue() {
        Some(marshalled) => {
            let value = unmarshal(marshalled, &mut actor.capabilities)?;
            continue_with_value(actor, value)
        }
        None => {
            actor.status = ActorStatus::Blocked;
            MachineEvent::Blocked
        }
    }
}
```

</details>
