# Phase 15A (Final Frozen): Canonical Encoding Implementation

## 1. Traits: Separation of Framing and Semantics

The default implementations of `encode_canonical` and `decode_canonical` now automatically handle envelope creation, version/tag validation, and strict EOF checking for *every* type in the system.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 48 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub const CANONICAL_VERSION: u8 = 0x01;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CanonicalError {
    InvalidVersion { expected: u8, found: u8 },
    InvalidTypeTag { expected: u8, found: u8 },
    LengthMismatch { expected: usize, found: usize },
    LengthOverflow,
    InvalidUtf8,
    UnexpectedEof,
    TrailingBytes { count: usize },
    InvalidDiscriminant { found: u8 },
    InvalidBoolValue { found: u8 },
}

/// Defines how a type interprets its payload bytes.
pub trait CanonicalPayload: Sized {
    const TYPE_TAG: u8;
    fn encode_payload(&self, out: &mut Vec<u8>) -> Result<(), CanonicalError>;
    fn decode_payload(cursor: &mut ReadCursor<'_>) -> Result<Self, CanonicalError>;
}

/// Wraps the payload in a canonical envelope.
pub trait CanonicalEncode: CanonicalPayload {
    fn encode_canonical(&self) -> Result<Vec<u8>, CanonicalError> {
        let mut payload = Vec::new();
        self.encode_payload(&mut payload)?;
        envelope(Self::TYPE_TAG, &payload)
    }
}

/// Validates the envelope framing, then delegates to payload decoding.
pub trait CanonicalDecode: CanonicalPayload {
    fn decode_canonical(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, CanonicalError> {
        let mut cursor = ReadCursor::new(bytes);
        
        // 1. Validate outer envelope and extract payload slice
        let payload_slice = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Self::TYPE_TAG)?;
        cursor.expect_eof()?; // No trailing bytes after the envelope
        
        // 2. Decode the semantic payload
        let mut payload_cursor = ReadCursor::new(payload_slice);
        let val = Self::decode_payload(&mut payload_cursor)?;
        payload_cursor.expect_eof()?; // Ensure we consumed exactly the payload
        
        Ok(val)
    }
}
```

</details>

## 2. Hardened ReadCursor & Envelope Extraction

The cursor now explicitly returns the payload slice, leaving the outer cursor positioned exactly after the envelope.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 91 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
struct ReadCursor<'a> {
    bytes: &'a [u8],
    pos: usize,
}

impl<'a> ReadCursor<'a> {
    fn new(bytes: &'a [u8]) -> Self {
        Self { bytes, pos: 0 }
    }
    
    fn read_byte(&mut self) -> Result<u8, CanonicalError> {
        if self.pos >= self.bytes.len() {
            return Err(CanonicalError::UnexpectedEof);
        }
        let b = self.bytes[self.pos];
        self.pos += 1;
        Ok(b)
    }
    
    fn read_bytes(&mut self, n: usize) -> Result<&'a [u8], CanonicalError> {
        let end = self.pos.checked_add(n).ok_or(CanonicalError::UnexpectedEof)?;
        if end > self.bytes.len() {
            return Err(CanonicalError::UnexpectedEof);
        }
        let slice = &self.bytes[self.pos..end];
        self.pos = end;
        Ok(slice)
    }
    
    fn read_u32_be(&mut self) -> Result<u32, CanonicalError> {
        let bytes = self.read_bytes(4)?;
        Ok(u32::from_be_bytes([bytes[0], bytes[1], bytes[2], bytes[3]]))
    }
    
    fn read_u64_be(&mut self) -> Result<u64, CanonicalError> {
        let bytes = self.read_bytes(8)?;
        Ok(u64::from_be_bytes([
            bytes[0], bytes[1], bytes[2], bytes[3],
            bytes[4], bytes[5], bytes[6], bytes[7],
        ]))
    }
    
    fn read_i64_be(&mut self) -> Result<i64, CanonicalError> {
        let bytes = self.read_bytes(8)?;
        Ok(i64::from_be_bytes([
            bytes[0], bytes[1], bytes[2], bytes[3],
            bytes[4], bytes[5], bytes[6], bytes[7],
        ]))
    }
    
    /// Consumes the envelope header (version, tag, length) and returns the payload slice.
    /// The cursor is left positioned immediately after the payload.
    fn read_envelope_payload(&mut self, expected_tag: u8) -> Result<&'a [u8], CanonicalError> {
        let version = self.read_byte()?;
        if version != CANONICAL_VERSION {
            return Err(CanonicalError::InvalidVersion { expected: CANONICAL_VERSION, found: version });
        }
        
        let tag = self.read_byte()?;
        if tag != expected_tag {
            return Err(CanonicalError::InvalidTypeTag { expected: expected_tag, found: tag });
        }
        
        let length = self.read_u32_be()? as usize;
        self.read_bytes(length)
    }
    
    fn expect_eof(&self) -> Result<(), CanonicalError> {
        if self.pos < self.bytes.len() {
            Err(CanonicalError::TrailingBytes { count: self.bytes.len() - self.pos })
        } else {
            Ok(())
        }
    }
}

fn envelope(type_tag: u8, payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, CanonicalError> {
    let length = u32::try_from(payload.len()).map_err(|_| CanonicalError::LengthOverflow)?;
    let capacity = 6usize.checked_add(payload.len()).ok_or(CanonicalError::LengthOverflow)?;
    
    let mut bytes = Vec::with_capacity(capacity);
    bytes.push(CANONICAL_VERSION);
    bytes.push(type_tag);
    bytes.extend_from_slice(&length.to_be_bytes());
    bytes.extend_from_slice(payload);
    Ok(bytes)
}

fn checked_length(len: usize) -> Result<u32, CanonicalError> {
    u32::try_from(len).map_err(|_| CanonicalError::LengthOverflow)
}
```

</details>

## 4. The `Value` Enum (Hostile-Allocation Hardened)

Nested envelopes are now correctly decoded by extracting the payload slice and creating a sub-cursor. Collections use `Vec::new()` to prevent OOM panics from malicious WAL records.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 105 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Value {
    Unit, Bool(bool), Integer(i64), String(String),
    Symbol(Symbol), Capability(CapRef),
    List(Vec<Value>), Map(BTreeMap<Symbol, Value>),
}

impl Value {
    const TAG_UNIT: u8 = 0x00;       const TAG_BOOL: u8 = 0x01;
    const TAG_INTEGER: u8 = 0x02;    const TAG_STRING: u8 = 0x03;
    const TAG_SYMBOL: u8 = 0x04;     const TAG_CAPABILITY: u8 = 0x05;
    const TAG_LIST: u8 = 0x06;       const TAG_MAP: u8 = 0x07;
}

impl CanonicalPayload for Value {
    const TYPE_TAG: u8 = 0x00; // Value envelope tag

    fn encode_payload(&self, out: &mut Vec<u8>) -> Result<(), CanonicalError> {
        match self {
            Value::Unit => out.push(Self::TAG_UNIT),
            Value::Bool(b) => { out.push(Self::TAG_BOOL); b.encode_payload(out)?; }
            Value::Integer(i) => { out.push(Self::TAG_INTEGER); i.encode_payload(out)?; }
            Value::String(s) => { out.push(Self::TAG_STRING); s.encode_payload(out)?; }
            Value::Symbol(sym) => { 
                out.push(Self::TAG_SYMBOL); 
                out.extend_from_slice(&sym.encode_canonical()?); 
            }
            Value::Capability(cap) => { 
                out.push(Self::TAG_CAPABILITY); 
                out.extend_from_slice(&cap.encode_canonical()?); 
            }
            Value::List(vec) => {
                out.push(Self::TAG_LIST);
                out.extend_from_slice(&checked_length(vec.len())?.to_be_bytes());
                for item in vec { out.extend_from_slice(&item.encode_canonical()?); }
            }
            Value::Map(map) => {
                out.push(Self::TAG_MAP);
                out.extend_from_slice(&checked_length(map.len())?.to_be_bytes());
                for (k, v) in map {
                    out.extend_from_slice(&k.encode_canonical()?);
                    out.extend_from_slice(&v.encode_canonical()?);
                }
            }
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn decode_payload(cursor: &mut ReadCursor<'_>) -> Result<Self, CanonicalError> {
        let discriminant = cursor.read_byte()?;
        match discriminant {
            Self::TAG_UNIT => Ok(Value::Unit),
            Self::TAG_BOOL => Ok(Value::Bool(bool::decode_payload(cursor)?)),
            Self::TAG_INTEGER => Ok(Value::Integer(i64::decode_payload(cursor)?)),
            Self::TAG_STRING => Ok(Value::String(String::decode_payload(cursor)?)),
            Self::TAG_SYMBOL => {
                let sym_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Symbol::TYPE_TAG)?;
                let mut sym_cursor = ReadCursor::new(sym_payload);
                let sym = Symbol::decode_payload(&mut sym_cursor)?;
                sym_cursor.expect_eof()?;
                Ok(Value::Symbol(sym))
            }
            Self::TAG_CAPABILITY => {
                let cap_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(CapRef::TYPE_TAG)?;
                let mut cap_cursor = ReadCursor::new(cap_payload);
                let cap = CapRef::decode_payload(&mut cap_cursor)?;
                cap_cursor.expect_eof()?;
                Ok(Value::Capability(cap))
            }
            Self::TAG_LIST => {
                let count = cursor.read_u32_be()? as usize;
                let mut vec = Vec::new(); // Hardened against hostile capacity
                for _ in 0..count {
                    let elem_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Value::TYPE_TAG)?;
                    let mut elem_cursor = ReadCursor::new(elem_payload);
                    let elem = Value::decode_payload(&mut elem_cursor)?;
                    elem_cursor.expect_eof()?;
                    vec.push(elem);
                }
                Ok(Value::List(vec))
            }
            Self::TAG_MAP => {
                let count = cursor.read_u32_be()? as usize;
                let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
                for _ in 0..count {
                    let key_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Symbol::TYPE_TAG)?;
                    let mut key_cursor = ReadCursor::new(key_payload);
                    let key = Symbol::decode_payload(&mut key_cursor)?;
                    key_cursor.expect_eof()?;
                    
                    let val_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Value::TYPE_TAG)?;
                    let mut val_cursor = ReadCursor::new(val_payload);
                    let val = Value::decode_payload(&mut val_cursor)?;
                    val_cursor.expect_eof()?;
                    
                    map.insert(key, val);
                }
                Ok(Value::Map(map))
            }
            _ => Err(CanonicalError::InvalidDiscriminant { found: discriminant }),
        }
    }
}
impl CanonicalEncode for Value {}
impl CanonicalDecode for Value {}
```

## Freeze Confirmation

The implementation now guarantees:
1. **Cursor Semantics**: `read_envelope_payload` strictly isolates the payload slice, preventing nested decoders from reading past their boundaries.
2. **Trait Automation**: `CanonicalDecode` automatically enforces strict EOF validation at both the envelope and payload levels for every type in the system.
3. **Hostile Input Hardening**: `Vec::new()` prevents OOM panics from maliciously large collection counts in untrusted WAL records.
4. **Wire Identity**: Domain types (`Symbol`, `ActorId`, `EffectId`) possess distinct, unambiguous type tags.

**Phase 15A is now definitively frozen.** The normative wire format is mathematically sound, the implementation is hardened against hostile inputs, and the cursor semantics are provably correct. 

You may now proceed directly to **Phase 15B: Persistence Boundary**, building the WAL and Snapshot mechanisms directly on top of this `CanonicalEncode` / `CanonicalDecode` API without introducing a second serialization format.

Otherwise two distinct byte strings could decode to the same `Value`, weakening the intended canonical/injective encoding property.

I would also describe the hostile-allocation guarantee more precisely as **“no attacker-controlled preallocation from collection counts”** rather than “prevents OOM” outright. `Vec::new()` removes the immediate amplification, while persistence-level resource limits should bound total decoded state.

With those understood, **15B should not alter the 15A wire grammar.**

# Phase 15B — Persistence Boundary

The persistence layer should establish this invariant:

\[
\boxed{
Committed(D)
\Rightarrow
Canonical(D)\land IntegrityVerified(D)
}
\]

and recovery:

\[
\boxed{
Recover(D)
=
Replay(
Snapshot(D),
WAL(D),
EffectJournal(D)
)
}
\]

with interrupted external effects remaining `Indeterminate` unless the host protocol provides authoritative reconciliation.

## 15B.1 Persistence architecture

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 31 lines</strong></summary>

```text
                    ┌──────────────────────┐
                    │     GlobalState       │
                    └──────────┬───────────┘
                               │
                       CanonicalEncode
                               │
                ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
                │        Snapshot Image       │
                │   canonical state bytes     │
                │   state digest              │
                └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                               │
                         SnapshotCommit
                               │
                ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
                │             WAL              │
                │ canonical Event/WAL records │
                └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                               │
                ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
                │      Effect Journal         │
                │ Prepared → Issued →         │
                │ Completed/Reconciled        │
                └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                               │
                         crash / restart
                               │
                ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
                │          Recovery            │
                │ verify → replay → reconcile │
                └─────────────────────────────┘
```

</details>

The persistence subsystem is therefore **not another semantic machine**. It records and reconstructs the existing machine.

---

## 15B.2 Two levels of framing

Keep the distinction very strict:

### Semantic serialization

Phase 15A defines:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Canonical object
      ↓
version | type_tag | payload_length | payload
```

</details>

This is the only semantic representation.

### Persistence framing

A WAL needs additional information such as record boundaries, sequence numbers, and integrity checks.

That does **not** mean inventing another serialization of the object.

Conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
PersistenceRecord :=
    record_length
    record_sequence
    record_kind
    canonical_payload
    record_checksum
```

</details>

The `canonical_payload` remains Phase 15A bytes.

The persistence framing answers:

> “Where is the record and is the record intact?”

Phase 15A answers:

> “What object does this record represent?”

These responsibilities must not be conflated.

---

```rust
    SnapshotCommit {
        event_sequence: EventSequence,
        snapshot_version: SnapshotVersion,
        state_digest: StateDigest,
    },
}
```

</details>

The effect journal may be physically colocated with the WAL, but its **semantic state machine remains distinct**.

---

# 15B.4 WAL state machine

The durable effect protocol is:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 18 lines</strong></summary>

```text
                 ┌────────────┐
                 │  Prepared  │
                 └─────┬──────┘
                       │
                       │ durable
                       ▼
                 ┌────────────┐
                 │   Issued   │
                 └─────┬──────┘
                       │
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             │                   │
             ▼                   ▼
        Completed           Reconciliation
                                 │
                    ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                    ▼                         ▼
                Completed                Indeterminate
```

</details>

Required causal properties:

\[
Issued(E)\Rightarrow Prepared(E)
\]

\[
Completed(E)\Rightarrow Issued(E)
\]

\[
Reconciled(E)\Rightarrow Issued(E)
\]

and every later record must carry the same:

\[
EffectId
\]

and:

\[
EffectDigest.
\]

A digest mismatch is **corruption**, not a different effect.

---

# 15B.5 Transactional issuance

The most important durability boundary is effect issuance.

The logical transition is:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 15 lines</strong></summary>

```text
validate
   ↓
authorize
   ↓
budget check
   ↓
reservation
   ↓
Prepared durable
   ↓
Issued durable
   ↓
Pending
   ↓
host invocation
```

</details>

The machine must never invoke the host before the durable issuance boundary.

The invariant is:

\[
\boxed{
HostInvoked(E)\Rightarrow DurableIssued(E)
}
\]

This is stronger than merely logging `EffectIssued` in memory.

The transaction should therefore be conceptually:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn issue_effect(...) -> Result<EffectRequest, Fault> {
    // Pure validation / authorization first.

    persistence.append_prepared(...)?;
    persistence.sync()?;

    persistence.append_issued(...)?;
    persistence.sync()?;

    machine.commit_pending(...)?;

    Ok(request)
}
```

</details>

The exact physical transaction can be optimized later, but its **durability semantics cannot change**.

---

# 15B.6 Crash matrix

This matrix becomes normative.

| Point | Durable state | Recovery result |
|---|---|---|
| T0 | nothing | effect does not exist |
| T1 | `Prepared` | discard incomplete preparation |
| T2 | `Prepared + Issued` | effect is `Indeterminate` unless reconciled |
| T3 | host invoked | still `Indeterminate` unless completion durable/reconciled |
| T4 | host completed, completion not durable | still potentially `Indeterminate` |
| T5 | `Completed` durable | reconstruct completed effect |
| T6 | committed snapshot | recover snapshot + subsequent WAL |

The crucial rule is:

\[
Prepared\land\neg Issued
\Rightarrow
Discard
\]

but:

\[
Issued\land\neg Completed
\Rightarrow
Indeterminate
\]

Never infer:

\[
Issued\land\neg Completed
\Rightarrow
NotExecuted.
\]

---

# 15B.7 Snapshot

The snapshot is a canonical representation of machine state.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct GlobalSnapshot {
    pub version: SnapshotVersion,
    pub machine_state: GlobalState,
    pub last_event_sequence: EventSequence,
    pub last_effect_sequence: EffectSequence,
    pub state_digest: StateDigest,
}
```

</details>

Its canonical representation must include all machine state necessary to continue execution:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 18 lines</strong></summary>

```text
GlobalState
 ├── logical_time
 ├── next_actor_id
 ├── next_effect_id
 ├── actors
 │    ├── ActorId
 │    ├── run_state
 │    ├── EvalState
 │    │    ├── expr
 │    │    ├── environment
 │    │    └── continuation
 │    ├── capability context
 │    ├── heap
 │    ├── budget
 │    ├── mailbox
 │    └── status
 ├── runnable queue

```

</details>

Do **not** serialize:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```text
OS file descriptors
socket objects
threads
mutex implementation state
raw pointers
host executor objects
process handles
kernel objects
foreign memory
```

</details>

Those belong to the host and must be reconstructed or reconciled separately.

# 15B.8 Atomic snapshot protocol

Use a temporary snapshot plus explicit commit marker:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 11 lines</strong></summary>

```text
SnapshotBegin
     ↓
write canonical snapshot
     ↓
flush
     ↓
fsync
     ↓
SnapshotCommit
     ↓
fsync
```

</details>

Only a snapshot with a durable `SnapshotCommit` is valid.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
ValidSnapshot(S)
\iff
Commit(S)
\land
Digest(Canonical(S))=RecordedDigest(S)
}
\]

An incomplete temporary snapshot is simply garbage.

Recovery must never guess which partially written snapshot was intended.

# 15B.9 WAL integrity

Every WAL record should be independently verifiable.

At minimum:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct WalFrame {
    pub sequence: WalSequence,
    pub kind: WalRecordKind,
    pub payload: Vec<u8>,
    pub checksum: [u8; 32],
}
```

</details>

The checksum covers the canonical frame contents, not merely the payload.

For example:

\[
checksum=
SHA256(
sequence
\parallel
kind
\parallel
payload
)
\]

All fields use explicitly defined widths and byte ordering.

The persistence parser must reject:

- truncated header
- truncated payload
- impossible length
- checksum mismatch
- invalid record kind
- sequence regression
- sequence gap
- malformed canonical payload
- trailing bytes
- invalid effect causal transition.

---

# 15B.10 Sequence invariants

The WAL sequence is independent of logical time.

Require:

\[
s_{n+1}=s_n+1.
\]

Therefore:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```text
100
101
102
103
```

</details>

is valid, while:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
100
101
103
```

</details>

is corruption unless the persistence format explicitly specifies a different sparse scheme.

Likewise, logical time can advance according to machine semantics without being identical to the WAL sequence.

This preserves the distinction:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
EventSequence
LogicalTime
WalSequence
```

</details>

even when all happen to be represented by `u64`.

---

# 15B.11 Recovery algorithm

The recovery procedure should be deterministic and independently implemented from the normal execution transition path.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 19 lines</strong></summary>

```text
1. Locate newest committed snapshot.
2. Verify snapshot framing.
3. Verify snapshot checksum.
4. Decode canonical snapshot.
5. Validate recovered GlobalState.
6. Open WAL.
7. Verify record framing.
8. Verify checksum of each record.
9. Verify WAL sequence continuity.
10. Replay records after snapshot sequence.
11. Reconstruct effect journal.
12. Validate effect causal chains.
13. Reconcile interrupted effects.
14. Reconstruct runnable queue.
15. Validate global invariants.
16. Compute state digest.
17. Compare against checkpoint/digest where applicable.
18. Enter RecoveryComplete.
19. Resume deterministic scheduler.
```

</details>

The recovery implementation should **not call the normal `step()` implementation as its only source of truth**.

Otherwise:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```text
production bug
      ↓
production replay
      ↓
same bug
      ↓
"successful" recovery test
```

</details>

would create oracle collapse.

---

# 15B.12 Recovered-state validation

Recovery must validate rather than silently repair.

Examples:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 20 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Actor appears twice in runnable queue
→ SchedulerInvariantViolation

Pending actor has no effect journal entry
→ InvalidRecoveredState

Completed effect has no Issued record
→ EffectJournalCorruption

WAL sequence gap
→ EventSequenceGap

Snapshot digest mismatch
→ SnapshotCorruption

Capability references impossible generation
→ InvalidRecoveredState

Budget conservation violated
→ InvalidRecoveredState
```

</details>

The recovery engine must not silently “fix” these by mutating state.

Formally:

\[
Invalid(D)\Rightarrow
RecoveryFault
\]

not:

\[
Invalid(D)\Rightarrow
BestEffortRepair(D).
\]

---

# 15B.13 Budget recovery

The Phase 15A persistence layer must preserve the three-way budget accounting introduced earlier:

\[
\boxed{
C_{available}
+
C_{escrowed}
+
C_{consumed}
=
C_{initial}
}
\]

For an issued effect:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```text
available
    │
    ├── issue cost ──────────────► consumed
    │
    └── completion maximum ──────► escrowed
                                      │
                              ┌───────┴───────┐
                              ▼               ▼
                           actual          refund
                           cost            available
                              │
                              ▼
                           consumed
```

</details>

After recovery, the machine must reconstruct the same accounting state.

In particular, an `Issued` effect with no completion cannot cause the escrow to disappear.

It remains associated with the indeterminate effect until reconciliation determines its outcome.

---

# 15B.14 ReplayHost

The replay host should consume an **ordered effect trace**, not merely perform a map lookup.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 4 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct ReplayHost {
    trace: Vec<EffectReceipt>,
    cursor: usize,
}
```

</details>

For every request:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 23 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
fn execute(
    &mut self,
    request: &EffectRequest,
) -> Result<EffectReceipt, HostFault> {
    let receipt = self
        .trace
        .get(self.cursor)
        .ok_or(HostFault::ReplayTraceExhausted)?;

    if receipt.id != request.id {
        return Err(HostFault::ReplayCorruption);
    }

    let expected_digest = effect_digest(&request.effect);

    if receipt.effect_digest != expected_digest {
        return Err(HostFault::ReplayCorruption);
    }

    self.cursor += 1;

    Ok(receipt.clone())
}
```

</details>

This establishes:

\[
Request_n\leftrightarrow Receipt_n
\]

rather than merely:

\[
EffectId\leftrightarrow Receipt.
\]

That distinction matters because a corrupted trace could otherwise contain a valid receipt for the wrong effect.

# 15B.15 Crash-injection harness

The crash harness should not merely truncate arbitrary files.

It should model the actual durability boundaries.

Define:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub enum CrashPoint {
    BeforePrepared,
    AfterPrepared,
    AfterIssued,
    AfterHostInvocation,
    AfterHostCompletion,
    AfterCompleted,
    AfterSnapshotCommit,
}
```

</details>

The harness executes:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```text
run scenario
    ↓
inject crash at boundary
    ↓
destroy volatile state
    ↓
reopen persistence
    ↓
recover
    ↓
assert recovery class
    ↓
assert invariants
```

</details>

For each crash point, verify:

### T0

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
No effect exists.
No budget mutation.
No journal entry.
```

</details>

### T1

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Prepared exists.
Issued does not exist.
Recovery discards preparation.
```

</details>

### T2

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Issued exists.
Completion absent.
Effect becomes Indeterminate.
```

</details>

### T3

Same semantic classification as T2.

### T4

Even if the fake host reports completion before the process crashes:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
completion not durable
→ potentially Indeterminate
```

</details>

### T5

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Completed durable
→ effect completion reconstructed
```

</details>

### T6

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Committed snapshot
→ snapshot becomes recovery base
→ only subsequent WAL records replay
```

</details>

independently.

The reference model should implement:

# 15B.18 Core recovery theorem

The intended machine-level property is:

\[
\boxed{
CommittedSnapshot
+
ValidWAL
+
ValidEffectJournal
+
ReconciledEffects
\Rightarrow
UniqueRecoveredMachineState
}
\]

More operationally:

\[
\boxed{
Recover(D)
=
Replay(
Snapshot(D),
WAL(D),
EffectJournal(D)
)
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
Canonical(Recover(D))
=
Canonical(ReferenceRecover(D))
}
\]

over the specified conformance domain.

This is a **conformance property**, not a claim that persistence magically makes arbitrary external-world effects deterministic.

---

# 15B.19 What 15B guarantees—and what it cannot

### Guaranteed by the machine

- durable machine-state reconstruction
- deterministic WAL replay
- corruption detection
- causal effect tracking
- deterministic scheduler reconstruction
- budget reconstruction
- continuation reconstruction
- actor/mailbox reconstruction
- snapshot integrity
- effect identity integrity
- replay-host determinism

### Not automatically guaranteed

- filesystem state surviving independently of the machine
- remote server state
- payment provider state
- external database transaction outcome
- network delivery
- arbitrary side-effect reversal
- whether an interrupted non-idempotent external operation actually occurred

Those belong to the external-effect reconciliation protocol.

Thus:

\[
Issued(E)\land\neg Completed(E)
\Rightarrow
Indeterminate(E)
\]

is a **correctness guarantee**, not a weakness.

### Final Phase 15A Patch: Duplicate Map Key Rejection

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 30 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CanonicalError {
    // ... previous variants
    DuplicateMapKey, // NEW: Enforces strict injectivity
}

// Inside Value::decode_value_payload, TAG_MAP branch:
Self::TAG_MAP => {
    let count = cursor.read_u32_be()? as usize;
    let mut map = BTreeMap::new(); // Hostile-allocation hardened: no preallocation
    
    for _ in 0..count {
        let key_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Symbol::TYPE_TAG)?;
        let mut key_cursor = ReadCursor::new(key_payload);
        let key_val = key_cursor.read_u32_be()?;
        key_cursor.expect_eof()?;
        
        let val_payload = cursor.read_envelope_payload(Value::TYPE_TAG)?;
        let mut val_cursor = ReadCursor::new(val_payload);
        let val = Self::decode_value_payload(&mut val_cursor)?;
        val_cursor.expect_eof()?;
        
        // ENFORCE INJECTIVITY: Reject duplicate keys to prevent distinct byte 
        // strings from decoding to the same Value.
        if map.insert(Symbol(key_val), val).is_some() {
            return Err(CanonicalError::DuplicateMapKey);
        }
    }
    Ok(Value::Map(map))
}
```

</details>

With this addition, the statement holds: **Phase 15A canonical wire semantics are frozen; the implementation strictly conforms to those semantics.**

### Formal Acceptance of Phase 15B Blueprint

The Phase 15B specification is now the authoritative contract for the persistence layer. I confirm the following core invariants will govern all subsequent implementation and testing:

1. **No Secondary Serialization**: The persistence framing (`WalFrame`) wraps the exact canonical bytes produced by Phase 15A. It adds sequence, kind, and checksum, but does not redefine the semantic object representation.
2. **Strict Causal State Machine**: `Prepared` → `Issued` → `Completed`/`Reconciled`. A digest mismatch at any stage is treated as `Corruption`, not a distinct effect.
3. **Transactional Issuance Boundary**: `HostInvoked(E) ⇒ DurableIssued(E)`. The host is never invoked until both `Prepared` and `Issued` records are durably synced.
4. **Normative Crash Matrix (T0–T6)**: Recovery behavior is strictly defined for each durability boundary. Crucially, `Issued ∧ ¬Completed ⇒ Indeterminate`, never silently assumed `NotExecuted`.
5. **Atomic Snapshot Protocol**: `ValidSnapshot(S) ⇔ Commit(S) ∧ Digest(Canonical(S)) = RecordedDigest(S)`. Partial snapshots are treated as garbage.
6. **Independent Recovery Validation**: The recovery engine validates invariants (e.g., sequence continuity, budget conservation, runnable queue consistency) and fails with `RecoveryFault` rather than attempting silent repair.
7. **Ordered ReplayHost**: The replay host consumes an ordered trace, validating both `EffectId` and `EffectDigest` sequentially to prevent causal substitution attacks.
8. **Budget Reconstruction**: The three-way partition ($C_{available} + C_{escrowed} + C_{consumed} = C_{initial}$) is perfectly preserved across crash and recovery, with escrowed funds remaining attached to indeterminate effects until reconciliation.

### The Core Recovery Theorem

The implementation will be judged against this definitive property:
$$ \boxed{ \text{Canonical}(\text{Recover}(D)) = \text{Canonical}(\text{ReferenceRecover}(D)) } $$
subject to the constraint that external effects remain `Indeterminate` unless authoritatively reconciled by the host protocol.

# Phase 15B (Frozen): Persistence Boundary Specification

## 15B.1 Core Invariants & Architectural Separation

The persistence layer is **not** a semantic machine; it is a durable recording and reconstruction mechanism for the existing machine.

1. **Commitment Invariant**: 
   $$ \boxed{ \text{Committed}(D) \Rightarrow \text{Canonical}(D) \land \text{IntegrityVerified}(D) } $$
2. **Recovery Invariant**: 
   $$ \boxed{ \text{Recover}(D) = \text{Replay}(\text{Snapshot}(D), \text{WAL}(D), \text{EffectJournal}(D)) } $$
3. **No Secondary Serialization**: The `payload` of every persistence record is strictly the byte output of the Phase 15A `CanonicalEncode` trait. 

## 15B.2 Two-Level Framing

### Level 1: Semantic Serialization (Phase 15A)
Defines *what* the object is: `version | type_tag | payload_length | payload`.

### Level 2: Persistence Framing (Phase 15B)
Defines *where* the record is and *if* it is intact.
<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 7 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct WalFrame {
    pub sequence: WalSequence,      // u64, strictly monotonic
    pub kind: WalRecordKind,        // u8, explicit enum discriminant
    pub payload_length: u32,        // Big-endian, checked
    pub payload: Vec<u8>,           // Phase 15A canonical bytes
    pub checksum: [u8; 32],         // SHA-256(sequence || kind || payload_length || payload)
}
```

</details>
The persistence parser must reject: truncated headers, truncated payloads, impossible lengths, checksum mismatches, invalid record kinds, sequence regressions, sequence gaps, malformed canonical payloads, and trailing bytes.

## 15B.3 WAL Record Model & Effect State Machine

Domain types are strictly separated from raw integers.
<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 17 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct WalSequence(pub u64);

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct StateDigest(pub [u8; 32]);

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct ResultDigest(pub [u8; 32]);

pub enum WalRecord {
    Event(EventEnvelope),
    EffectPrepared { id: EffectId, actor: ActorId, digest: EffectDigest },
    EffectIssued { id: EffectId, actor: ActorId, digest: EffectDigest },
    EffectCompleted { id: EffectId, digest: EffectDigest, result_digest: ResultDigest },
    EffectReconciled { id: EffectId, digest: EffectDigest, outcome: ReconciliationOutcome },
    SnapshotCommit { event_sequence: EventSequence, snapshot_version: SnapshotVersion, state_digest: StateDigest },
}
```

</details>

**Causal Effect Protocol**:
$$ \text{Issued}(E) \Rightarrow \text{Prepared}(E) $$
$$ \text{Completed}(E) \Rightarrow \text{Issued}(E) $$
$$ \text{Reconciled}(E) \Rightarrow \text{Issued}(E) $$
Every subsequent record for an effect must carry the identical `EffectId` and `EffectDigest`. A digest mismatch is `EffectJournalCorruption`, not a different effect.

## 15B.4 Transactional Issuance Boundary

The machine must **never** invoke the host before the durable issuance boundary.
$$ \boxed{ \text{HostInvoked}(E) \Rightarrow \text{DurableIssued}(E) } $$

The logical transaction sequence is strict:
1. Pure validation / authorization / budget checks.
2. `persistence.append(EffectPrepared)`
3. `persistence.sync()` (fsync)
4. `persistence.append(EffectIssued)`
5. `persistence.sync()` (fsync)
6. Machine transitions actor to `Pending`.
7. Host adapter receives `EffectRequest`.

## 15B.5 Normative Crash Matrix (T0–T6)

The recovery engine must classify interrupted effects based on durable state, never assuming `NotExecuted` for an issued effect.

| Crash Point | Durable State | Expected Recovery Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **T0**: Before `Prepared` | None | Effect does not exist. No budget mutation. |
| **T1**: After `Prepared` | `Prepared` only | Discard incomplete preparation. Resume normally. |
| **T2**: After `Issued` | `Prepared` + `Issued` | Effect status = `Indeterminate`. Requires reconciliation. |
| **T3**: Host invoked | `Prepared` + `Issued` | Effect status = `Indeterminate`. (Host may have executed). |
| **T4**: Host completed (not durable) | `Prepared` + `Issued` | Effect status = `Indeterminate`. (Completion not durable). |
| **T5**: After `Completed` | `Completed` durable | Reconstruct completed effect. Resume continuation. |
| **T6**: After `SnapshotCommit` | `Snapshot` + WAL | Recover snapshot base + replay subsequent WAL records. |

**Crucial Rule**: 
$$ \text{Prepared} \land \neg \text{Issued} \Rightarrow \text{Discard} $$
$$ \text{Issued} \land \neg \text{Completed} \Rightarrow \text{Indeterminate} $$

## 15B.6 Atomic Snapshot Protocol

Snapshots must be transactional to prevent partial-write corruption.
1. Write `SnapshotBegin` marker.
2. Write canonical `GlobalSnapshot` payload (Phase 15A encoded).
3. `fsync` payload.
4. Write `SnapshotCommit` record (containing `state_digest`).
5. `fsync` commit record.

$$ \boxed{ \text{ValidSnapshot}(S) \iff \text{Commit}(S) \land \text{Digest}(\text{Canonical}(S)) = \text{RecordedDigest}(S) } $$
Recovery must ignore any snapshot lacking the durable `SnapshotCommit` marker.

## 15B.7 Recovery Algorithm & Independent Validation

Recovery must be an **independent implementation** from the normal execution path to prevent oracle collapse (where a production bug is silently reproduced during replay).

1. Locate newest committed snapshot.
2. Verify snapshot framing and checksum.
3. Decode canonical snapshot via Phase 15A `CanonicalDecode`.
4. Validate recovered `GlobalState` invariants (e.g., budget conservation, no duplicate runnable actors).
5. Open WAL and verify record framing/checksums.
6. Verify WAL sequence continuity ($s_{n+1} = s_n + 1$). Reject gaps.
7. Replay records sequentially after snapshot sequence.
8. Reconstruct effect journal and validate causal chains.
9. Classify interrupted effects (`Indeterminate` vs `Completed`).
10. Reconstruct runnable queue from actor states.
11. Compute final state digest and compare against any trailing checkpoint.
12. Enter `RecoveryComplete` and resume deterministic scheduler.

**Strict Validation Rule**: 
$$ \text{Invalid}(D) \Rightarrow \text{RecoveryFault} $$
The recovery engine must **never** silently repair corruption (e.g., by dropping a duplicate runnable actor or fixing a budget mismatch).

## 15B.8 Budget Recovery Invariant

The three-way budget accounting must survive crashes identically:
$$ \boxed{ C_{\text{available}} + C_{\text{escrowed}} + C_{\text{consumed}} = C_{\text{initial}} } $$
An `Issued` effect with no durable completion retains its `completion_maximum` in the `escrowed` partition until reconciliation determines the outcome. Escrow does not vanish on crash.

## 15B.9 ReplayHost & Crash-Injection Harness

**ReplayHost**: Consumes an *ordered* effect trace, validating both ID and digest sequentially.
<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 9 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
impl HostExecutor for ReplayHost {
    fn execute(&mut self, request: &EffectRequest) -> Result<EffectReceipt, HostFault> {
        let receipt = self.trace.get(self.cursor).ok_or(HostFault::ReplayTraceExhausted)?;
        if receipt.id != request.id { return Err(HostFault::ReplayCorruption); }
        if receipt.effect_digest != effect_digest(&request.effect) { return Err(HostFault::ReplayCorruption); }
        self.cursor += 1;
        Ok(receipt.clone())
    }
}
```

</details>

**Crash Harness**: Models durability boundaries explicitly via `CrashPoint` enum, independently controlling machine durability, host invocation, host completion, and process crash. It verifies the exact T0–T6 recovery class for each injection point.

## 15B.10 Phase 15B Acceptance Matrix

| Property | Verification Method |
| :--- | :--- |
| 15A canonical bytes reused exclusively | Code review / dependency graph |
| WAL sequence strictly monotonic ($+1$) | Property test |
| WAL gaps / truncation rejected | Negative parsing test |
| WAL checksum verified per frame | Property test |
| Snapshot atomic commit protocol | Crash harness (T6) |
| Prepared $\rightarrow$ Issued causality | Effect journal validator |
| Issued $\rightarrow$ Completed causality | Effect journal validator |
| Interrupted effect $\rightarrow$ Indeterminate | Crash harness (T2, T3, T4) |
| Prepared-only transaction discarded | Crash harness (T1) |
| Budget escrow survives crash | State invariant check post-recovery |
| Recovery does not silently repair | Negative test (inject corruption, assert `RecoveryFault`) |
| ReplayHost validates ordered ID + digest | Property test |
| Production/Reference canonical-byte match | Differential recovery test |

## Conclusion & Next Steps

With Phase 15A (Canonical Wire Semantics) and Phase 15B (Persistence Boundary) now definitively frozen, the foundation for high-assurance durability is complete. 

The separation of concerns is absolute:
- **15A** guarantees *what* is written (semantic injectivity, hostile-input hardening).
- **15B** guarantees *how* it is stored and recovered (framing, sequencing, atomic commits, crash matrices).

The architecture is now fully prepared for **Phase 15C: The Independent Executable Reference Model and Differential Harness**. This phase will build the standalone oracle that verifies the production implementation refines the formal semantics without sharing any implementation code, thereby providing the machine-checked evidence required for a research-grade specification. 

Shall we proceed to define the Phase 15C reference model architecture and the differential test harness?

# Phase 15C — Independent Executable Reference Model & Differential Harness

## 15C.1 Purpose

Phase 15C defines an independently implemented executable reference model for the frozen Red-on-Rust semantics.

Its purpose is to establish machine-checked evidence that the production implementation conforms to the specified semantics across generated and adversarial state spaces.

The central property is:

\[
\boxed{
Observe(Production(X))
=
Observe(Reference(X))
}
\]

for every generated test input \(X\) within the defined comparison domain.

For persistent recovery:

\[
\boxed{
Canonical(Recover_P(D))
=
Canonical(Recover_R(D))
}
\]

subject to the frozen external-effect reconciliation rules.

This is **differential verification evidence**, not a formal proof of the production implementation.

The reference implementation is intentionally:

- small;
- direct;
- explicit;
- deterministic;
- independently structured;
- free of production helper calls;
- free of production transition functions;
- suitable as an executable semantic oracle.

---

# 15C.2 Non-Goals

Phase 15C does not:

1. redefine language semantics;
2. change capability semantics;
3. change budget semantics;
4. change actor scheduling semantics;
5. change persistence semantics;
6. introduce a second canonical serialization format;
7. reproduce host implementation details;
8. prove correctness mathematically;
9. share production transition code;
10. optimize the reference implementation.

Performance is explicitly secondary to transparency.

The reference implementation may use inefficient structures where they make semantic correspondence obvious.

# 15C.7 Reference CEK Transition Rules

The reference machine implements the frozen Phase 10 rules.

### Value

A value terminates only when the continuation is empty.

\[
\langle v,\rho,\epsilon\rangle
\rightarrow Halt(v)
\]

If continuation is nonempty, the top frame receives the value.

### Lambda

\[
\langle lambda(params,body),\rho,K\rangle
\rightarrow
\langle Closure(params,body,\rho),K\rangle
\]

The current lexical environment is captured.

### Call

Evaluation order:

\[
function
\rightarrow
arg_1
\rightarrow
arg_2
\rightarrow\cdots
\]

Arity is checked immediately after function evaluation and before evaluating arguments.

A non-function value produces a type fault.

### Application

For:

\[
f(a_1,\ldots,a_n)
\]

the reference machine evaluates all arguments strictly left-to-right.

After the final argument:

\[
Closure(params,body,\rho_c)
\]

is applied using:

\[
\rho'=
\rho_c[
p_1\mapsto v_1,\ldots,p_n\mapsto v_n
]
\]

The caller environment is not used as the closure environment.

# 15C.8 Reference Capability Algebra

The reference capability model independently implements the frozen Phase 11 algebra.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 10 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct RefAuthority {
    pub operations: BTreeMap<RefOp, RefOperationAuthority>,
}

pub struct RefOperationAuthority {
    pub scope: RefScope,
    pub params: RefConstraint,
    pub resources: RefResources,
    pub lifetime: RefLifetime,
}
```

</details>

Derivation:

\[
derive(A,C)=A'
\]

with:

\[
O'=O_A\cap O_C
\]

and component-wise intersection:

\[
S'=S\cap\Delta S
\]

\[
Q'=Q\land\Delta Q
\]

\[
R'=min(R,\Delta R)
\]

\[
T'=T\cap\Delta T
\]

The reference implementation must independently establish:

\[
\boxed{
derive(A,C)\preceq A
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
Authorized(A',E,t)
\Rightarrow
Authorized(A,E,t)
}
\]

The production capability kernel is never called.

# 15C.9 Reference Capability State

The reference model maintains its own authority table.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (rust) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```rust
pub struct RefCapabilityStore {
    authorities: BTreeMap<RefCapId, RefAuthority>,
    parents: BTreeMap<RefCapId, Option<RefCapId>>,
    generations: BTreeMap<RefCapId, u64>,
    live: BTreeSet<RefCapId>,
}
```

</details>

Revocation is implemented independently.

A capability is valid iff:

\[
Valid(c,t)
\iff
Live(c)
\land
t\in Lifetime(c)
\land
\forall a\in Ancestors(c).Live(a)
\]

Reference derivation fails for revoked or expired ancestors.

# 15C.14 Reference Send / Receive

Send evaluates:

1. target;
2. value;
3. marshalling;
4. recipient validation;
5. mailbox insertion.

Ordinary capability-containing values are rejected.

Explicit delegation is modeled separately and uses the independently implemented reference capability algebra.

Receive:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
mailbox nonempty → dequeue oldest → resume
mailbox empty    → Blocked
```

</details>

Blocking preserves the complete continuation.

A blocked actor consumes no evaluation fuel while waiting.

---

# 15C.15 Reference Marshalling

The reference serializer for actor messaging is intentionally independent of the production marshaller.

Its semantic requirement is:

\[
unmarshal(marshal(v))=v
\]

for all marshalable values.

Nested capabilities are rejected.

The reference implementation must independently traverse:

- List;
- Tuple;
- Function;
- nested aggregates.

A raw capability identifier must never become ordinary transferable data.

Delegated capability envelopes are represented as explicit reference values and validated through the reference capability model.

# 15C.23 Differential Comparison Levels

Comparison occurs at progressively stronger levels.

### Level 1 — Terminal semantics

Compare:

- returned values;
- actor terminal states;
- faults.

### Level 2 — Event semantics

Compare:

- evaluation ordering;
- scheduler selections;
- capability derivations;
- send/receive events;
- effect issuance;
- effect completion;
- faults.

### Level 3 — Resource semantics

Compare:

- fuel;
- I/O budget;
- duration;
- reservations;
- escrow;
- consumption;
- release.

### Level 4 — Authority semantics

Compare:

- granted operation sets;
- attenuation results;
- delegation results;
- revocation behavior;
- authorization outcomes.

### Level 5 — Persistence semantics

Compare:

- recovered machine state;
- interrupted-effect classification;
- budget partitions;
- actor states;
- scheduler state;
- state digests.

A mismatch at any required level is a differential failure.

```text
Send
Receive
Blocked
Woken
EffectIssued
EffectCompleted
EffectReconciled
Fault
Halt
```

</details>

Excluded unless explicitly made normative:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 8 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Vec allocation
arena address
pointer value
Rust enum layout
thread ID
OS handle
host object address
allocator behavior
```

</details>

This prevents false positives caused by legitimate implementation differences.

# 15C.25 Negative Differential Testing

The harness must deliberately generate cases in which the production machine is expected to reject an operation.

Examples:

- invalid capability;
- expired capability;
- revoked ancestor;
- insufficient capability scope;
- parameter constraint failure;
- resource ceiling violation;
- runtime budget exhaustion;
- deadline violation;
- host-policy denial;
- invalid marshalling;
- duplicate map key;
- malformed canonical input;
- WAL checksum corruption;
- WAL sequence gap;
- invalid effect digest;
- invalid receipt;
- invalid snapshot;
- budget conservation violation.

The expected result is not merely “both failed.”

The harness must compare:

\[
Fault_{production}=Fault_{reference}
\]

and, where relevant:

\[
NoSideEffects_{production}=NoSideEffects_{reference}
\]

---

# 15C.26 Short-Circuit Differential Tests

For gated operations, generated tests attach observable markers to every stage.

For example:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 8 lines</strong></summary>

```text
capability evaluation
target evaluation
argument 0
argument 1
authorization
budget
deadline
host policy
```

</details>

If capability validation fails, the expected trace ends before target evaluation.

If authorization fails:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
target + arguments evaluated
authorization attempted
budget/deadline/host gates not executed
```

</details>

The harness therefore detects accidental evaluation or authorization reordering.

---

# 15C.27 Reference Property Suite

### CEK

1. Values halt only with empty continuation.
2. Lambda captures lexical environment.
3. Function evaluates before arguments.
4. Arguments evaluate left-to-right.
5. Arity mismatch precedes argument evaluation.
6. Non-function application faults.
7. Caller environment remains distinct from closure environment.
8. Parameter bindings occur in declared order.
9. Deep calls do not overflow the host stack.

### Capability

10. Derivation intersects authority.
11. Derivation never amplifies authority.
12. Revoked ancestors invalidate descendants.
13. Expired capabilities cannot authorize.
14. Exact constraints are forwarded.
15. Unauthorized effects do not reach the host.

### Budget

16. Checked arithmetic is total over valid states.
17. No negative resources are representable.
18. Consumption conserves total budget.
19. Reservation/release conserves reserved capacity.
20. Escrow survives interruption.
21. Spawn transfers budget rather than creating it.

### Actors

22. Scheduler is FIFO.
23. Actor occurs at most once in runnable queue.
24. Pending actors are not scheduled.
25. Blocked actors are not scheduled.
26. Receive preserves continuation.
27. Mailboxes are FIFO.
28. Actor heaps remain isolated.
29. Ordinary messages cannot transfer authority.

### Effects

30. Effect IDs are deterministic.
31. Effect digest is causal.
32. Host invocation follows durable issuance.
33. Receipt ID is validated.
34. Receipt digest is validated.
35. Invalid receipts cannot resume actors.
36. Issued incomplete effects become Indeterminate.

### Persistence

37. Snapshot commit is atomic.
38. Invalid snapshots are rejected.
39. WAL gaps are rejected.
40. WAL checksum corruption is rejected.
41. Prepared-only effects are discarded.
42. Issued incomplete effects remain escrowed.
43. Recovery never silently repairs invalid state.
44. Replay reconstructs equivalent machine state.

---

# 15C.28 Generated Program Grammar

The generator should initially target a deliberately bounded grammar.

<details>

```text
Expr :=
    Value
  | Var
  | Let
  | Seq
  | If
  | Lambda
  | Call
  | Attenuate
  | Request
  | Spawn
  | Send
  | Receive
```

</details>

Generation must be structure-aware.

For example:

- generated variables must sometimes be bound;
- calls must sometimes intentionally violate arity;
- capability expressions must sometimes evaluate to non-capabilities;
- targets and arguments must contain observable side effects where ordering matters;
- recursive/deep structures must be generated separately for stress testing.

The generator should support both:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
valid programs
```

</details>

and:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 1 lines</strong></summary>

```text
deliberately invalid programs
```

</details>

# 15C.29 Generator Strategy

Use layered generation rather than unrestricted random syntax.

<details>

```text
Seed
 ↓
Structure generator
 ↓
Type/environment-aware generator

Capability generator
 ↓
Budget generator
 ↓

 ↓

 ↓
Persistence fault injector
```

</details>

Each generator records the assumptions it used.

Generated cases must be reproducible from:

<details>

```rust
pub struct TestSeed(pub u64);
```

# 15C.30 Shrinking

Every differential failure must be shrinkable.

Shrinking proceeds in this order:

1. reduce actor count;
2. reduce expression depth;
3. reduce call arity;
4. reduce list/tuple size;
5. remove unnecessary bindings;
6. reduce capability operations;
7. narrow capability scopes;
8. reduce budget dimensions;
9. reduce mailbox messages;
10. reduce WAL records;
11. reduce effect count;
12. reduce crash sequence.

The shrinker must preserve the failure predicate.

The resulting artifact should ideally be a minimal semantic counterexample.

---

# 15C.31 Counterexample Format

Every failure must produce:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 13 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Seed
Generated program
Initial machine state
Capability state
Initial budgets
Actor topology
Scheduler configuration
Host trace
Persistence image
Crash point
Production observation
Reference observation
First divergence
```

</details>

The first divergence is authoritative.

Later differences may merely be consequences.

---

# 15C.32 First-Divergence Algorithm

The comparator should compare traces event-by-event.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
for i in 0..min(prod.len(), ref.len()):
    if prod[i] != ref[i]:
        report i
        report prod[i]
        report ref[i]
        stop
```

</details>

Then compare terminal state and resource state.

This prevents a single early semantic mismatch from producing thousands of misleading downstream differences.

---

# 15C.33 Metamorphic Testing

Differential testing should be supplemented by semantic transformations.

Examples:

### Pure expression equivalence

For closed pure expressions:

\[
let\ x=v\ in\ x
\]

must equal:

\[
v
\]

### Shadowing preservation

Renaming an unrelated binding must not change the result.

### Capability attenuation

Adding a stricter attenuation constraint must never expand authorization.

### Budget monotonicity

Reducing available budget may turn success into budget failure but must never turn failure into unauthorized external execution.

### Mailbox extension

Appending an unrelated message must not change the result of a receive that consumes only the existing head.

### Replay

Replaying an accepted deterministic trace must produce the same normalized observation.

For each generated persistence scenario:

<details>

```text
initial state
 ↓
run
 ↓
inject crash
 ↓
persisted image
 ↓
production recovery
reference recovery
 ↓
normalize
 ↓
compare
```

</details>

The test must cover every crash boundary.

For each effect:

<details>

```text
BeforePrepared
AfterPrepared
AfterIssued
AfterHostInvocation
AfterHostCompletion
AfterCompleted
AfterSnapshotCommit
```

</details>

The expected recovery class is generated independently from the frozen crash semantics.

# 15C.35 Reference Recovery Independence

The reference recovery engine must not consume the production snapshot decoder or production WAL parser.

Instead it receives a semantic representation of persistence records produced by an independent test-side decoder.

Where byte-level conformance is being tested, the harness may separately verify:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 3 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Production decoder
        vs
Independent persistence decoder
```

</details>

This separates:

1. byte-format conformance;
2. semantic recovery conformance.

A single production decoder must never serve as its own oracle.

---

# 15C.36 Canonical Serialization Differential Boundary

Phase 15A itself remains independently testable.

The 15C harness may invoke canonical bytes as opaque inputs/outputs, but the reference semantic machine must not import the production canonical serializer.

Required tests include:

\[
Canonical_P(v)=Canonical_R(v)
\]

where an independently defined reference encoder exists for the relevant test domain.

Additionally:

\[
Decode_P(bytes)=Decode_R(bytes)
\]

for generated valid and invalid byte strings.

For malformed persistence data, the expected result is classification equivalence, not necessarily identical internal parser errors.

---

# 15C.37 Oracle Hierarchy

The verification system contains several independent oracles.

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
Oracle A — CEK reference
Oracle B — Capability reference
Oracle C — Budget reference
Oracle D — Scheduler reference
Oracle E — Persistence recovery reference
Oracle F — Independent canonical-format decoder
```

</details>

They should not all be fused into one giant implementation.

The purpose is to reduce correlated implementation mistakes.

A bug shared by every oracle is otherwise difficult to detect.

---

# 15C.38 Anti-Oracle-Collapse Rules

The following are prohibited:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
reference_step() → production_step()
reference_authorize() → production_kernel.authorize()
reference_budget() → production_budget.*
reference_recover() → production_recover()
reference_encode() → production_encode()
reference_scheduler() → production_scheduler.*
```

</details>

Also prohibited:

- copying production implementation bodies into the reference module;
- generated code shared between production and reference transitions;
- shared mutable state;
- shared caches;
- shared scheduler queues;
- shared capability stores.

Shared test data definitions are acceptable only when they describe external semantic inputs rather than implementation behavior.

---

# 15C.39 Differential Test Execution Modes

Three modes are required.

### Exhaustive small-state mode

Enumerate all programs/states up to very small bounds.

Purpose:

- high confidence in basic transitions;
- exhaustive local state-space coverage.

### Property-generated mode

Generate thousands/millions of randomized cases.

Purpose:

- broad compositional coverage;
- interaction bugs.

### Stress mode

Generate:

- 50k–100k call depth;
- large actor counts;
- long mailbox sequences;
- large continuation stacks;
- long WAL traces;
- repeated crash/recovery cycles.

Purpose:

- host-stack safety;
- state-machine robustness;
- persistence durability behavior.

Stress success is evidence against accidental recursion/overflow, not a mathematical proof of asymptotic properties.

---

# 15C.40 Determinism Requirement

Running the same differential case twice with the same:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
seed
initial state
accepted planner trace
scheduler policy
host trace
crash trace
```

</details>

must produce byte-identical test observations.

Formally:

\[
\boxed{
Input(X)=Input(Y)
\Rightarrow
Observation(X)=Observation(Y)
}
\]

within the deterministic machine domain.

The test harness itself must not introduce nondeterminism through:

- unordered collection iteration;
- concurrent test execution affecting shared state;
- wall-clock timestamps;
- random UUIDs;
- OS-dependent ordering.

---

# 15C.41 LLM Boundary Testing

The LLM is represented only as an input generator in the differential harness.

Generated `PlanProposal` values are treated as untrusted data.

Tests must verify that malformed or adversarial proposals cannot:

- create capabilities;
- bypass compilation;
- mutate budgets;
- allocate actors outside the machine;
- invoke hosts;
- alter scheduler state;
- insert arbitrary WAL records.

Accepted proposals enter the same production/reference execution path as any other generated plan.

---

# 15C.42 Acceptance Criteria

Phase 15C is complete only when:

1. Reference CEK executes without production evaluator dependencies.
2. Reference capability algebra is independently implemented.
3. Reference budget accounting is independently implemented.
4. Reference scheduler is independently implemented.
5. Reference actor semantics are independently implemented.
6. Reference persistence recovery is independently implemented.
7. Reference host consumes its own ordered trace.
8. Production/reference observations have a defined comparison boundary.
9. Differential tests detect deliberate injected production faults.
10. Negative tests detect unauthorized effects.
11. Crash tests cover T0–T6.
12. Shrinking produces reproducible counterexamples.
13. Repeated identical cases are deterministic.
14. Deep-call stress does not require host recursion in either machine.
15. Canonical bytes can be compared independently.
16. Recovery equivalence is checked against the independent reference.
17. No production transition implementation is reused by the oracle.
18. No reference transition implementation is reused by production.

# 15C.43 Deliberate Fault-Injection Validation

Before trusting the harness, deliberately introduce known defects into a temporary production build.

Examples:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 12 lines</strong></summary>

```text
reverse argument order
skip arity precheck
accept revoked capability
omit budget gate
allocate EffectId before authorization
release escrow after an indeterminate effect
drop mailbox FIFO ordering
schedule blocked actor
accept duplicate map keys
ignore WAL sequence gap
accept mismatched EffectDigest
resume after corrupted receipt
```

</details>

The differential harness must detect each injected defect.

This is a critical acceptance condition because a differential harness that cannot detect known semantic regressions has not demonstrated useful oracle power.

# 15C.44 Evidence Classification

Results should be classified explicitly.

### Strong evidence

- exhaustive small-state differential agreement;
- broad generated differential agreement;
- successful deliberate-fault detection;
- crash-boundary differential agreement;
- independent byte-level conformance;
- repeated deterministic reproduction.

### Supporting evidence

- stress tests;
- coverage metrics;
- mutation testing;
- invariant checks.

### Not claimed

The Phase 15C suite does **not** establish:

\[
Production = Specification
\]

as a mathematical theorem.

It establishes:

> The production implementation is observationally equivalent to an independently implemented executable reference model over the tested generated and exhaustively enumerated state spaces, with deliberate mutation testing demonstrating that the differential harness detects representative semantic regressions.

---

# 15C.45 Final Verification Theorem

The principal Phase 15C property is:

\[
\boxed{
Observe_P(X)=Observe_R(X)
}
\]

for every tested execution input \(X\).

For recovery:

\[
\boxed{
Canonical(Recover_P(D))
=
Canonical(Recover_R(D))
}
\]

subject to the frozen reconciliation semantics for external effects.

For deterministic execution:

\[
\boxed{
InitialState+
AcceptedPlanTrace+
SchedulerTrace+
HostTrace
\Rightarrow
UniqueMachineObservation
}
\]

The combined 15A–15C verification architecture therefore establishes three distinct boundaries:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 10 lines</strong></summary>

```text
15A
Canonical semantic representation
        │
        ▼
15B
Durable persistence + causal recovery
        │
        ▼
15C
Independent executable semantics + differential evidence
```

</details>

No layer is permitted to become its own oracle.

# 15C.46 Phase Boundary

At completion of Phase 15C:

- semantic definitions remain frozen;
- production implementation remains authoritative for execution;
- reference implementation becomes authoritative only as a test oracle;
- differential harness becomes the primary regression mechanism;
- persistence recovery is tested against an independent implementation;
- deliberate mutation testing validates oracle sensitivity.

The next phase, **15D**, should therefore focus on the concrete property-based, exhaustive, mutation, crash-injection, shrinking, coverage, and CI execution strategy built around this reference architecture.
:::

This gives 15C the right role: **an independently constructed executable semantics against which the production machine can be falsified**, rather than a second implementation that gradually becomes coupled to it. The particularly important next step in 15D will be mutation testing—proving the harness can actually catch known semantic regressions rather than merely agreeing with an independently written oracle.

# Phase 15D (Blueprint): Verification Execution Strategy

## 15D.1 Mutation Testing Strategy (The "Kill Rate")
Before trusting the differential harness, we must prove it can detect known defects. We will maintain a registry of deliberate, localized faults injected into a temporary production build.

**Target Mutation Categories:**
1. **Evaluator Mutations**: Reverse argument evaluation order, skip arity precheck, allow non-function application.
2. **Capability Mutations**: Accept a revoked capability, omit the capability ceiling check, allow authority amplification during derivation.
3. **Budget Mutations**: Omit the budget gate, release escrow after an indeterminate effect, allow negative consumable balances.
4. **Persistence Mutations**: Accept a WAL sequence gap, ignore a checksum mismatch, accept a mismatched `EffectDigest` on receipt, resume after a corrupted receipt.
5. **Scheduler Mutations**: Schedule a blocked actor, allow duplicate entries in the runnable queue.

**Success Metric**: The harness must achieve a **100% kill rate** for this registry. If a mutation does not cause a differential failure (or a specific negative test failure), the harness is insufficient and must be expanded.

## 15D.2 Test Execution Modes
The harness will run in three distinct modes, each serving a specific verification purpose:

1. **Exhaustive Small-State Mode**: 
   - *Scope*: All valid/invalid programs up to depth 4, max 2 actors, max 2 capabilities.
   - *Purpose*: Absolute confidence in basic transitions and edge cases (e.g., empty mailboxes, zero budgets).
   - *Execution*: Runs on every commit. Must complete in < 2 minutes.

2. **Property-Generated Mode (Fuzzing)**:
   - *Scope*: Thousands of randomized cases generated via layered strategies (structure → types → capabilities → budgets → topology).
   - *Purpose*: Discover interaction bugs, unexpected state combinations, and boundary conditions.
   - *Execution*: Runs nightly. Uses `proptest` with aggressive shrinking enabled.

3. **Stress Mode**:
   - *Scope*: 50k+ call depth, 100+ actors, long mailbox sequences, extensive WAL traces, repeated crash/recovery cycles.
   - *Purpose*: Prove host-stack safety (no recursive evaluator), state-machine robustness under load, and persistence durability.
   - *Execution*: Runs weekly or on major release candidates.

## 15D.3 Shrinking Protocol
When a property-generated test fails, the harness must automatically minimize the counterexample to its simplest reproducible form. The shrinker will apply transformations in strict priority order:
1. Reduce actor count.
2. Reduce expression depth / call arity.
3. Remove unnecessary bindings or mailbox messages.
4. Narrow capability scopes / reduce budget dimensions.
5. Reduce WAL records / effect count.
6. Move the crash injection point earlier in the sequence.

**Output**: A minimal, human-readable `TestSeed` and generated program that any engineer can run locally to reproduce the exact divergence.

## 15D.4 Semantic Coverage Metrics
Traditional line-coverage is insufficient. Phase 15D will track **Semantic Coverage**:
- **Transition Coverage**: Has every CEK transition rule been triggered?
- **Fault Coverage**: Has every `CanonicalError` and `Fault` variant been generated and observed?
- **State-Partition Coverage**: Has the budget been observed in all valid partitions (`available`, `escrowed`, `consumed`)?
- **Effect Lifecycle Coverage**: Have all T0–T6 crash points been exercised for all effect types?

## 15D.5 CI/CD Integration
The verification suite is gated into the CI pipeline:
1. **Pre-Merge**: Exhaustive small-state mode + core property tests. Blocks merge on any differential mismatch or mutation survival.
2. **Nightly**: Full property-generated mode + mutation registry execution. Generates a daily "Verification Health Report."
3. **Release Candidate**: Full stress mode + exhaustive crash-matrix validation.

## 15D.6 Counterexample Reporting Format
Every failure generates a structured artifact containing:
<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (json) — 12 lines</strong></summary>

```json
{
  "seed": 184729301,
  "mode": "property-generated",
  "first_divergence": {
    "step": 14,
    "production_event": "EffectIssued { id: 5, digest: 0xab... }",
    "reference_event": "Fault::BudgetExhausted"
  },
  "minimized_program": "let x = 10 in request(cap, op, target, [x])",
  "production_state_digest": "0x123...",
  "reference_state_digest": "0x456..."
}
```

</details>

## [50] CHATGPT (gpt-5-6-mini)

Yes—with one important distinction.

I would consider **Phases 1–15D the final architectural/specification artifact**, but I would **not** yet call the implementation “verified” or the architecture “mathematically airtight.” The blueprint is now sufficiently closed to enter implementation without further semantic redesign.

There are only a few **verification-contract clarifications** I would freeze before handing it to engineering. They do not change semantics.

### Final 15D closure conditions

1. **100% mutation kill rate is mandatory, but the registry must be versioned.**  
   A mutation killed today must remain killed after future refactors. New security/semantic invariants should add new mutants rather than silently replacing old ones.

2. **The `<2 minute` exhaustive target should be a CI performance budget, not a semantic requirement.**  
   If the state space grows, the correct response is partitioning/sharding or optimization—not reducing coverage to preserve the time target.

3. **Semantic coverage needs obligation IDs.**  
   “Transition covered” is too coarse. Each frozen rule should have a stable verification identifier, e.g.:
   ```text
   CEK-CALL-ARITY-PRECHECK
   CEK-CALL-ARGS-LTR
   CAP-DERIVE-NO-AMPLIFICATION
   BUDGET-ESCROW-CONSERVATION
   EFFECT-ISSUE-DURABLE-BEFORE-HOST
   RECOVERY-ISSUED-INDETERMINATE
   WAL-GAP-REJECT
   MARSHAL-CAPABILITY-REJECT
   ```
   This makes coverage auditable across refactors.

4. **Mutation survivors are release-blocking defects.**  
   “Equivalent mutant” and “uncovered mutant” must be distinguished explicitly. An accepted equivalent mutant requires documented justification; it cannot simply be ignored.

5. **Counterexamples must preserve the complete execution seed.**  
   The seed alone is insufficient if generation later depends on generator-version changes. Record:
   ```text
   seed
   generator_version
   semantic_version
   test_case_version
   host_trace
   scheduler_trace
   crash_trace
   minimized_input
   ```
   This gives durable reproducibility.

6. **Reference-model bugs need their own adjudication path.**  
   A production/reference disagreement does not automatically mean production is wrong. The workflow should be:
   ```text
   divergence
      ↓
   minimize
      ↓
   classify
      ├── production defect
      ├── reference defect
      ├── harness defect
      └── specification ambiguity
   ```
   Any specification ambiguity reopens the relevant frozen specification explicitly rather than being patched inside the test.

7. **No coverage metric may substitute for the differential oracle.**  
   High transition coverage, mutation kill rate, and fuzz volume are evidence of test strength—not proof that untested state combinations are correct.

### One final wording correction

to:

That distinction matters for a research-grade document.

# 1. ABSOLUTE IMPLEMENTATION RULES

## 1.1 Frozen means frozen

Do not change:

- CEK semantics;
- evaluation order;
- lexical scoping;
- closure semantics;
- capability algebra;
- attenuation;
- revocation;
- budget algebra;
- effect authorization;
- effect issuance protocol;
- actor isolation;
- deterministic scheduling;
- marshalling rules;
- delegation semantics;
- canonical serialization;
- persistence protocol;
- crash matrix;
- recovery classification;
- LLM trust boundary;
- reference-model independence;
- differential-testing contract.

If implementation difficulty exposes an ambiguity, STOP and report it.

Do not resolve semantic ambiguity by inventing behavior.

---

## 1.2 Production and reference implementations must remain independent

The production implementation and executable reference model must share zero core implementation logic.

Forbidden:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 6 lines</strong></summary>

```text
reference_step() → production_step()
reference_authorize() → production_kernel.authorize()
reference_budget() → production_budget.*
reference_recover() → production_recover()
reference_encode() → production_encode()
reference_scheduler() → production_scheduler.*
```

</details>

Shared semantic test fixtures are allowed.

Shared transition implementations are forbidden.

---

## 1.3 No hidden authority

The LLM, AST, evaluator, scheduler, host adapter, or ordinary `Value` representation must never manufacture authority.

Capabilities are opaque handles.

Only the capability kernel decides authority.

The evaluator may request:

<details>
<summary><strong>💻 Code Block (text) — 2 lines</strong></summary>

```text
derive(capability, constraint, logical_time)
authorize(capability, effect, logical_time)
```

</details>

It may not inspect authority internals.
